name: Leviticus
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: Yahweh{a} called out to Moses{b} from the tent of meeting{c} and gave him these words for the people.
“Tell the people of Israel: Anyone who wants to bring a gift{d} to Yahweh must choose an animal from his own cattle or his own flock.
Suppose the gift is a burnt offering{e} from the cattle. Then the animal must be a male with no flaw. The worshiper leads it to the doorway of the meeting tent, so that Yahweh will accept him.{f}
He must rest his hand on the animal’s head.{g} Then it will be accepted in his place, to pay for his wrongs.{h}
The man kills the bull there in front of Yahweh. Aaron’s sons, who are the priests, carry the blood forward and throw it against all sides of the altar by the entrance of the tent of meeting.{i}
The worshiper takes off the skin and cuts the animal into pieces.
The priests, Aaron’s sons, light a fire on the altar and lay wood on top of it.
Next they set the pieces on the wood over the fire, with the head and the fat{j} placed among them.
The worshiper must wash the insides and the legs in water. Then the priest turns everything into smoke on the altar. This is a burnt offering, a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.{k}
“If the gift for a burnt offering comes from the flock, whether a sheep or a goat, it must also be a male with nothing wrong with it.
He kills it on the altar’s north side, facing Yahweh. Then the priests, who are Aaron’s sons, splash its blood on every side of the altar.
The animal is cut into pieces. The priest lays them on the wood over the altar fire, with the head and the fat in place.
The insides and the legs are washed in water. Then the priest brings the whole animal and burns it on the altar. It is a burnt offering, a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.
“If the burnt offering for Yahweh is a bird, the worshiper must choose either a dove or a young pigeon.
The priest takes the bird to the altar and twists off its head. He burns the head on the altar, and the blood is squeezed out on the altar’s side.
He pulls out the stomach and its contents{l} and tosses them on the east side of the altar, in the place where ashes are dumped.{m}

Then he tears the bird open by its wings, but he does not pull it apart. The priest burns it on the wood over the altar fire. It is a burnt offering, a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.”

notes.text: Hebrew YHWH, the personal name of God. This Bible writes it as “Yahweh” everywhere. See the note at Exodus 3:15.
Moses is probably an Egyptian name meaning “son.” In Hebrew it sounds like “drawn out” (Exodus 2:10).
Hebrew ohel moed. This was the tent where Yahweh met with Moses and with Israel (Exodus 25:22; 40:34-35).
Hebrew qorban, from a verb meaning “to come near.” It is something brought near to God.
Hebrew olah, “that which goes up,” because the whole animal went up in smoke.
Or “so that it will be accepted for him.” The Hebrew can mean either the animal or the worshiper.
The hand may have shown that the animal belonged to the worshiper. Scholars disagree on the exact meaning.
Hebrew kipper, often translated “atone.” Its basic meaning is debated: to cover, to wipe away, or to pay a ransom.
Hebrew zaraq, to throw liquid out of a bowl.
Hebrew peder, a word found only here and in 8:20. It is probably the fat around the inner organs.
Literally “a soothing smell.” The phrase means that God accepts the gift. It first appears in Genesis 8:21.
Or “its feathers.” The Hebrew word is uncertain, and the Septuagint says “feathers.”
Literally “the place of the fat ashes” (see 6:10-11).

verses.text: “When someone brings a grain offering{a} to Yahweh, the gift must be fine flour.{b} He pours olive oil over the flour and adds frankincense.{c}

He carries it to Aaron’s sons, the priests. One priest scoops out a handful of the flour and oil, with all of the frankincense, and burns it on the altar as the reminder portion.{d} It is a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.
Whatever remains of the grain goes to Aaron and his sons. Of all the gifts burned for Yahweh, this share is most sacred.
“If you bring a grain offering that was baked in an oven,{e} make it from fine flour mixed with oil. It may be loaves without yeast, or thin flat cakes brushed with oil.
If your grain offering was cooked on a flat pan, it is made of fine flour mixed with oil, and it has no yeast.
Crumble it into bits, then drizzle oil on top. That makes it a grain offering.
If your grain offering was cooked in a deep pan,{f} make it with fine flour and oil.
Bring the grain offering, made in any of these ways, to Yahweh. Hand it over to the priest, and he will carry it to the altar.
The priest takes out the reminder portion and burns it on the altar. It is a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.
Whatever remains of the grain goes to Aaron and his sons. Of all the gifts burned for Yahweh, this share is most sacred.
“No grain offering for Yahweh may be made with yeast. Never burn yeast or honey{g} as a gift to Yahweh.
You may bring them to Yahweh as the first share of your harvest,{h} but they must never be placed on the altar for a pleasing smell.
Put salt on every grain offering. Never leave out the salt that stands for God’s agreement with you.{i} Add salt to every offering you bring.
“If you bring Yahweh a grain offering from your first harvest, offer new heads of grain that have been roasted over a fire, then ground into coarse meal.{j}
Pour oil over it and lay frankincense on top. It is a grain offering.
The priest burns the reminder portion, which is some of the ground grain and some of the oil, along with all the frankincense. It is a gift made by fire for Yahweh.”

notes.text: Hebrew minchah. In other places it means any gift or tribute (Genesis 4:3-5). In the laws for priests it means a gift of grain, and that is how it is translated here.
Hebrew solet, probably the finest grade of wheat flour.
A sweet-smelling resin from trees that grow in southern Arabia and East Africa.
Hebrew azkarah, probably “reminder,” the part that brings the worshiper to God’s attention. Others say “token portion.”
Hebrew tannur, a clay oven heated from the inside. Dough was baked against its walls.
Hebrew marchesheth, probably a deeper pan than the flat pan of verse 5.
Hebrew devash. It may include fruit syrup, such as date syrup, as well as honey from bees. Both yeast and honey make things ferment.
Hebrew reshit, the first and best part of a harvest (see 23:10, 17).
Literally “the salt of the covenant of your God.” Salt keeps food from spoiling, so it stood for an agreement meant to last (Numbers 18:19).
Hebrew karmel, probably fresh, full heads of new grain. The exact way of preparing it is uncertain.

verses.text: “A person may bring a peace offering{a} from his cattle. It can be a bull or a cow, but it must have no flaw, and he presents it to Yahweh.
He rests a hand on its head and kills it at the doorway of the meeting tent. Then Aaron’s sons, the priests, splash the blood on every side of the altar.
From this peace offering the worshiper must give Yahweh a gift made by fire. It is the fat that covers the insides, and all the fat attached to them.
He also gives both kidneys, with the fat on them near the waist, and the best part of the liver.{b} The liver part is cut away together with the kidneys.
Aaron’s sons burn all of this on the altar, laid over the burnt offering that already lies on the wood and fire. It is a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.
“A person may bring a peace offering to Yahweh from the flock instead. It can be a ram or a ewe, but it must have no flaw.
If he brings a lamb, he leads it up in front of Yahweh.
He rests a hand on its head and kills it before the meeting tent. Aaron’s sons splash its blood on every side of the altar.

Out of this peace offering he gives Yahweh a gift made by fire. It is the animal’s fat, including the whole fat tail,{c} cut off right beside the spine. He also gives the fat covering the insides and all the fat attached to them.
He offers both kidneys, with the fat on them near the waist, and the liver’s best part, cut away together with the kidneys.
The priest burns it all on the altar as a meal{d} for Yahweh, a gift made by fire.
“A person may bring a goat. He leads it up in front of Yahweh.{e}
He rests a hand on its head and kills it before the meeting tent. Then Aaron’s sons splash its blood on every side of the altar.
From the goat he gives a gift made by fire for Yahweh. It is the fat covering the insides and everything attached to them.
Both kidneys go too, along with the fat on them near the waist and the liver’s best part, cut away together with the kidneys.
The priest burns all of it on the altar as a meal for Yahweh. This gift made by fire has a pleasing smell, and all fat is Yahweh’s.
This is a law for you that will never end, for every generation and in every home: you must never eat fat or blood.”

notes.text: Hebrew zevach shelamim. The word shelamim is related to shalom, “peace” or “well-being.” It is also called a fellowship offering. God received the fat, the priest received a share, and the worshiper ate the rest (7:11-36).
Hebrew yothereth, probably the lobe of the liver that sticks out.
The wide, fatty tail of Middle Eastern sheep. It can weigh many pounds.
Literally “the food of the gift made by fire.” Hebrew lechem means “bread” or “food.” It was an old way of speaking about offerings. The Bible also says that God does not need food (Psalm 50:12-13).
A Greek scroll of Leviticus found at Qumran writes God’s name here and in the next chapter as Iao, a Greek form of Yahweh, instead of “Lord.” It is early evidence that the name was spoken aloud.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the people of Israel: Suppose someone sins by mistake{a} and breaks one of Yahweh’s commands, doing something that was forbidden.
If it is the high priest,{b} who was anointed, and his sin brings guilt on the people, he must give Yahweh a young bull with no flaw. It is a sin offering{c} for the sin he committed.
He leads the bull to the doorway of the meeting tent, in front of Yahweh. He rests a hand on its head and kills it there before Yahweh.
Then the high priest takes a little of the bull’s blood into the meeting tent.
He dips a finger into it and flicks some blood seven times in front of Yahweh, toward the curtain of the holy place.

He smears some of the blood on the horns of the incense altar, which stands inside the meeting tent before Yahweh. The rest of the blood he pours out at the bottom of the burnt offering altar, at the doorway of the meeting tent.
He must cut out all the fat of the sin offering bull: the fat that covers the insides and all the fat attached to them,
He also takes out both kidneys and the fat on them by the waist, plus the liver’s best part, which is cut free along with the kidneys.
These parts are removed just as they are from an ox given as a peace offering. Then the priest burns them on the burnt offering altar.
The bull’s skin, all its meat, its head, its legs, its insides, and its waste
are different. He carries the whole animal outside the camp, to a clean place where the ashes are dumped. There he burns it on a wood fire, right on the ash heap.
“Now suppose the whole community of Israel does wrong without realizing it. The matter is hidden from them, yet they have broken one of Yahweh’s commands and are guilty.{d}
When they learn about the sin, the people must bring a young bull for a sin offering to the front of the meeting tent.
The elders rest their hands on the bull’s head in front of Yahweh, and someone kills the bull there before Yahweh.
The high priest then carries some of its blood into the meeting tent.
He dips a finger in the blood and flicks it seven times before Yahweh, toward the curtain.

He smears some blood on the horns of the altar that is inside the meeting tent before Yahweh. Whatever blood is left, he pours out at the bottom of the burnt offering altar at the entrance of the tent.
He cuts out every bit of the fat and burns it on the altar.
He treats this bull exactly as he treated the first sin offering bull. By doing this, the priest pays for the people’s wrongs, and they are forgiven.
He hauls the bull outside the camp and burns it, just as he did the first one. This offering is for the sin of the whole assembly.
“Now suppose a ruler{e} sins by mistake. He breaks one of the commands of Yahweh his God and does something forbidden, so he is guilty.
If he is told what he did wrong, he brings a male goat with no flaw as his gift.
He rests a hand on the goat’s head and kills it where burnt offerings are killed before Yahweh. It is a sin offering.
The priest dips his finger in some of the blood and smears it on the horns of the burnt offering altar. He pours the remaining blood out at the bottom of that altar.
He burns all the fat on the altar, as he does with the fat of a peace offering. In this way the priest pays for the ruler’s wrong, and the ruler is forgiven.
“Now suppose an ordinary person from the community{f} sins by mistake. He does something Yahweh has forbidden, and he is guilty.
When he is told what he did wrong, he brings a female goat with no flaw for the sin he committed.
He rests a hand on its head and kills it at the place for burnt offerings.
The priest dips a finger in the blood and smears it on the horns of the burnt offering altar. Whatever blood is left, he pours out at the base of that altar.
He cuts out all of the fat, just as the fat is cut from a peace offering, and burns it on the altar. Its smell pleases Yahweh. In this way the priest pays for the man’s wrong, and he is forgiven.
“If the person brings a lamb for his sin offering, it must be a female with no flaw.
He rests a hand on its head and kills it as a sin offering at the place for burnt offerings.
The priest dips a finger in some of the blood and smears it on the horns of the burnt offering altar. He pours the remaining blood out at the altar’s base.

He cuts out all the fat, the way the lamb’s fat is cut from a peace offering, and burns it on the altar over the gifts made by fire for Yahweh. Through this the priest pays for the sin the man committed, and he is forgiven.”

notes.text: Hebrew bishgagah, “by error.” It covers wrong done through not knowing the law, or by accident. Sin done on purpose and in defiance (“with a high hand,” Numbers 15:30) is not covered by these offerings.
Hebrew “the anointed priest,” the high priest (see 8:12; 21:10).

Hebrew chattat, the same word as “sin.” Some scholars call it a “purification offering,” because its blood cleansed the holy place and its objects from the stain of sin and uncleanness. It was also required where no wrong was done (12:6-8). “Sin offering” is kept here.
Hebrew asham. It can mean “be guilty,” “become guilty,” or “realize one’s guilt.” The same question comes up in verses 22 and 27 and in 5:2-5, 17.
Hebrew nasi, a tribal leader (Numbers 1:16; 7:2).
Hebrew am haarets, here the ordinary members of the community, as opposed to priests and leaders.

verses.text: “Suppose a person hears a public call to speak up as a witness.{a} He saw the matter or knows about it, but he says nothing. He has sinned, and he will carry the blame.
Or suppose someone touches something unclean without knowing it. It might be the body of a dead wild animal, a dead farm animal, or a dead swarming creature.{b} He is unclean and guilty.
Or suppose he touches a person’s uncleanness, of any kind that makes people unclean, and does not realize it. When he finds out, he is guilty.
Or suppose someone makes a hasty promise with an oath to do something, good or bad. People do speak rashly this way. He forgets it, but when he remembers, he is guilty.
Whenever a person is guilty in one of these ways, he must admit the sin he committed.
He brings Yahweh a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, as the payment{c} for his sin. This is a sin offering. The priest pays for his wrong.
“If he cannot afford a lamb,{d} he may bring two doves or two young pigeons to Yahweh as payment. One is a sin offering and one is a burnt offering.
He brings them to the priest, who offers the sin offering bird first. The priest twists its head at the neck, but does not tear it off.
He flicks some of the blood against the side of the altar and drains the remaining blood out at its base. This bird is the sin offering.
The second bird he offers as a burnt offering, following the usual rules. Through this the priest pays for the man’s sin, and he is forgiven.
“If he cannot afford even two doves or two young pigeons, he brings about 2 quarts{e} of fine flour as his sin offering. He must not add oil or frankincense, because this is a sin offering.
He takes it to the priest, who scoops out a handful as the reminder portion and burns it on top of the altar, on Yahweh’s gifts made by fire. It is a sin offering.
In this way the priest pays for the sin the man committed in any of these ways, and he is forgiven. As with a grain offering, the leftover flour belongs to the priest.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,

“Suppose someone betrays Yahweh’s trust{f} by sinning, without meaning to, against something holy that belongs to Yahweh. He must bring a ram from the flock with no flaw. Its worth in silver{g} is set by the standard of the holy place,{h} and it is a guilt offering.{i}
He must also pay back what he took from the holy thing, adding one fifth more, and give it to the priest. The priest pays for his wrong with the guilt offering ram, and he is forgiven.
“Suppose someone sins by doing something Yahweh has forbidden, even though he does not know it. He is guilty and will carry the blame.
He brings the priest a ram from the flock with no flaw, valued at the right price, as a guilt offering. The priest pays for the mistake he made without knowing, and he is forgiven.
This is a guilt offering. He truly was guilty before Yahweh.”{j}

notes.text: Literally “hears the voice of an oath.” This was a public curse or call put on anyone who knew about a crime and kept quiet (Judges 17:2; Proverbs 29:24).
Hebrew sherets, small creatures that swarm on land or in water (11:10, 20, 29).
Hebrew asham, here the payment owed. It is the same word as “guilt offering” in verses 14-19. The Septuagint says “for his trespass.”
Literally “if his hand cannot reach enough for a lamb.” This lower price for poor people shows up again in 12:8 and 14:21-32.
Hebrew “a tenth of an ephah,” about 2.2 liters or 2 quarts. Ancient measures varied.
Hebrew maal, treating something holy that belongs to God as if it were ordinary. It is a breach of trust against him.
Hebrew “in shekels of silver.” No number is given. The Hebrew plural may mean at least two shekels (about 0.8 ounce or 23 grams), or it may only mean “its worth in silver.”
Hebrew “by the shekel of the sanctuary,” a standard shekel of 20 gerahs (27:25; Exodus 30:13), about 0.4 ounce or 11.5 grams.
Hebrew asham, also called a “reparation offering,” because it goes with paying back for a wrong against God’s holy things or against a neighbor (6:1-7).
Or “He has truly made himself guilty before Yahweh.” The Septuagint says “for he has truly trespassed before the Lord.”

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,{a}

“Suppose someone betrays Yahweh’s trust by cheating a neighbor. Perhaps he lied about something left in his care or given as a pledge. Perhaps he stole, or squeezed money out of his neighbor by force.
Perhaps he found something lost and lied about it, or he swore a false oath. He may have done any of these wrongs.
When he is guilty, he must give back whatever he stole or took by cheating. He must return the item left in his care, or the lost thing he found,
or whatever he swore falsely about. He must pay for it in full and add one fifth of its worth. He hands this to the owner on the day he admits his guilt.{b}
Then he brings Yahweh his guilt offering, a ram from the flock with no flaw, worth the right price, and gives it to the priest.
The priest pays for his wrong before Yahweh, and the man is forgiven for whatever he did that made him guilty.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Command Aaron and his sons: Here is the teaching{c} on the burnt offering. Its pieces lie on the altar’s fireplace{d} through the night until dawn, and the altar fire is to keep burning on it.
The priest dresses in his linen robe and linen shorts. He scoops up the greasy ashes left when the fire burned the offering on the altar, and he sets them down next to the altar.
Then he changes into different clothes and carries the ashes outside the camp to a clean place.
The fire on the altar must keep burning. It must never go out. Every morning the priest adds wood, arranges the burnt offering on top, and burns the fat of the peace offerings over it.
Never let that fire die. It is to burn on the altar without a break.
“Now the teaching on the grain offering. Aaron’s sons bring it to Yahweh and set it in front of the altar.
One of them scoops up a handful of fine flour and oil, together with all the frankincense lying on the grain. On the altar he burns the reminder portion, and Yahweh enjoys its smell.
Aaron and his sons eat the rest, as flat bread made without yeast. They are to eat it in a holy place, which is the courtyard around the tent of meeting.
No yeast may go into it. I have given it to the priests as their portion of the gifts burned for me. It is most holy, the same as the sin offering and the guilt offering are.
Any man in Aaron’s family may eat some. This is a permanent rule for all your generations concerning Yahweh’s burned gifts. Whatever touches them becomes holy.”{e}
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,

“On the day Aaron and his sons are anointed,{f} each must give Yahweh this gift: about 2 quarts{g} of fine flour for a grain offering that is repeated daily. One half is offered at dawn, and the other half at dusk.
Cook it on a flat pan with oil. Bring it soaked well, and present the grain offering in pieces{h} so that its smell pleases Yahweh.
The priest from Aaron’s family who is anointed to take his place makes this offering. It belongs to Yahweh for all time, and all of it is burned.
Every grain offering from a priest must be burned completely. Nobody may eat it.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell Aaron and his sons: These are the rules for the sin offering. It must be killed in front of Yahweh, in the same place where burnt offerings are killed. It is most holy.
The priest who presents the sin offering is the one who eats it. He eats in a holy place, within the courtyard around the tent of meeting.
Whatever touches its meat becomes holy. If its blood spatters a piece of clothing, wash the stained cloth in a holy place.
Break any clay pot used for boiling the meat. A bronze pot may be kept, but it must be scrubbed and then rinsed in water.
Any man among the priests may eat it. It is most holy.
But if any of the blood was brought into the meeting tent to pay for wrongs in the holy place, the meat must not be eaten. Burn it up.”

notes.text: In the Hebrew Bible, verses 6:1-7 are numbered 5:20-26, and 6:8-30 are numbered 6:1-23. This Bible keeps the usual English numbering.
Or “on the day he brings his guilt offering.”
Hebrew torah, “instruction.” Here it means the steps of a ritual. The same word begins each section from 6:8 to 7:38.
Hebrew moqedah, “burning place.” It is found only here.

Or “Anyone who touches them must be holy.” Scholars disagree about whether holiness passes to whatever touches the gifts, or whether only people already holy may touch them (see verse 27 and Exodus 29:37).
Or “from the day he is anointed,” meaning a gift made every day after that. The Septuagint says “on the day you anoint him.”
Hebrew “a tenth of an ephah,” about 2.2 liters or 2 quarts. Ancient measures varied.
Hebrew tuphine, found only here. It may mean “baked pieces” or “broken pieces.”

verses.text: “Here is the teaching on the guilt offering, a most holy gift.
The animal is killed in the place where burnt offerings are killed. Its blood is splashed on every side of the altar.
The priest must present all its fat: the fat tail, the fat that wraps the stomach and intestines,
both kidneys with the fat on them near the waist, and the liver’s best part, cut away together with the kidneys.
The priest then burns them on the altar as a gift for Yahweh made by fire. That is the guilt offering.
Any man among the priests can eat the meat, as long as he eats it in a holy place. It is most holy.
The guilt offering and the sin offering have one rule. The meat goes to the priest who pays for the wrong with it.
When a priest offers someone’s burnt offering, the animal’s skin is his to keep.
A grain offering baked in an oven, or one cooked on a griddle or in a pan, goes to the priest who brings it.
Every other grain offering, oiled or dry, is divided evenly among Aaron’s sons.
“These are the rules for the peace offering that a person may bring to Yahweh.

If he brings it to give thanks,{a} he must bring bread along with the animal. It includes loaves with no yeast, mixed with oil, flat cakes with no yeast, spread with oil, and loaves of fine flour soaked in oil.
He must also bring loaves made with yeast, together with his thank offering.
One piece of each kind of bread is offered to Yahweh as a special gift{b}, and that piece belongs to the priest who throws the peace offering’s blood on the altar.
A thank offering’s meat has to be finished the day it is offered. None may stay until morning.
When the offering fulfills a promise or is a voluntary gift, it is eaten that same day, though any part left over can be eaten on the following day.
But any meat still left on the third day must be burned up.

If anyone eats meat from his peace offering on the third day, God will not accept it. The offering will not count for the one who brought it. It has become rotten,{c} and the person who eats it will carry the blame.
“Meat that touches anything unclean must not be eaten. Burn it up. As for the rest of the meat, anyone who is clean may eat it.
But anyone who eats meat from Yahweh’s peace offering while he is unclean must be cut off{d} from his people.

Suppose someone touches something unclean, such as human uncleanness, an unclean animal, or any unclean and hateful thing,{e} and then eats meat from Yahweh’s peace offering. That person must be cut off from his people.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the people of Israel: You must never eat the fat of an ox, a sheep, or a goat.
Fat from an animal that died on its own or was torn apart by wild animals may serve any other purpose. You may never eat it, though.
If someone eats fat from an animal that could have been presented to Yahweh as a burned gift, his people will cut him off.
In all your homes, never eat blood from any bird or animal.
If a person eats any blood at all, his people will cut him off.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the people of Israel: Whoever brings a peace offering to Yahweh must set aside part of it as his gift to Yahweh.
He must carry Yahweh’s gifts made by fire in his own hands. He brings the fat together with the breast, and the breast is lifted and swung before Yahweh as a wave offering.{f}
The priest burns the fat on the altar, but the breast goes to Aaron and his sons.
You must give the right thigh to the priest as a special gift from your peace offerings.
The son of Aaron who presents the blood and the fat of the peace offering receives the right thigh as his share.

Out of the peace offerings of the Israelites, I have kept back the breast that was swung and the thigh that was set apart. I give them to Aaron the priest and his sons as a portion that is theirs permanently.
This was Aaron’s and his sons’ portion of the gifts burned for Yahweh, given the day Moses{g} brought them forward to serve Yahweh as priests.
On the day he anointed them, Yahweh ordered the people of Israel to give them this share. It is theirs for all time, in every generation.”
That completes the teaching about the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering,{h} and the peace offering.
Yahweh commanded all this to Moses on Mount Sinai, when he told the Israelites to bring their offerings to Yahweh in the Sinai desert.

notes.text: Hebrew todah, “thanks” or “praise.” This was a peace offering given to thank God for being rescued (Psalm 107:22; 116:17).
Hebrew terumah, something set apart, literally “something lifted off.”
Hebrew piggul, a special word for sacrifice meat that is spoiled for use because it was kept too long (19:7; Isaiah 65:4).
Hebrew karath. Scholars disagree on whether it means being put to death by the community, dying early by God’s hand, or having no descendants.
Hebrew sheqets. Many Hebrew copies, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Syriac read sherets, “swarming creature,” as in 5:2.
Hebrew tenufah, a gift presented by moving it toward the altar and back, or by lifting it up.
Probably Moses (see 8:1-30). The Hebrew can also mean “on the day they were brought forward.”
Hebrew milluim, “filling,” from the phrase “fill the hand,” which means to put someone into priestly service (8:33; Exodus 29:9).

subheads.37: The end of the offering laws

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Take Aaron and his sons with their clothing. Bring the anointing oil, the sin offering bull, both rams, and the basket holding the bread made without yeast.
Gather the whole community at the doorway of the tent of meeting.”
Moses did what Yahweh ordered, and the people came together at the tent of meeting’s entrance.
Moses said to them, “Yahweh has ordered what we are about to do.”
Moses led Aaron and his sons up and bathed them in water.
Moses put the tunic on Aaron first, with the sash tied at his waist. Next came the robe and the ephod.{a} The ephod was held on by its woven belt.
Moses set the chest piece on Aaron and placed the Urim and Thummim{b} in it.
On Aaron’s head he put the turban, and on the front of the turban he fastened the gold plate, which is the holy crown.{c} Everything followed Yahweh’s orders to Moses.
Moses then picked up the anointing oil. He poured it over the tabernacle and everything in it, setting each thing apart for God.
He flicked some of the oil on the altar seven times, and he anointed the altar with all its tools, and the washing bowl with its stand, setting them apart.
He poured some of the oil on Aaron’s head to anoint him and set him apart.
Moses then brought Aaron’s sons forward. He dressed them in tunics, wrapped sashes around them, and tied caps on their heads, as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
Next the bull for the sin offering was led up, and Aaron and his sons pressed their hands against its head.

Moses killed the animal, collected its blood, and used his finger to smear some on each horn of the altar. By this he cleansed{d} the altar. The leftover blood he poured out at the altar’s foot. He set the altar apart and paid for its stain.
Moses took all the fat on the insides, the liver’s best part, and both kidneys with their fat, and burned them on the altar.
The rest of the bull, with its skin, meat, and waste, he burned in a fire outside the camp, as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
Then he led up the ram for the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons rested their hands on its head.
Moses killed it and splashed its blood on every side of the altar.
He cut the ram into pieces and burned the head, the pieces, and the fat.
Moses washed the stomach and legs in water, and he burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing smell, a gift burned for Yahweh, as Yahweh had commanded.
Next he led up the second ram, the ram for ordination. Aaron and his sons rested their hands on its head.
Moses killed it. With some of its blood he touched the lower edge of Aaron’s right ear, then Aaron’s right thumb, and then his right big toe.
Aaron’s sons were brought up next. Moses put blood on the edge of each one’s right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. The remaining blood he splashed all around the altar.
Moses took the fat, including the fat tail and every bit of fat on the insides. He took the liver’s best part, the two kidneys with their fat, and the right thigh as well.
From the basket of bread without yeast that sat before Yahweh, he picked up a plain loaf, a loaf made with oil, and a flat cake, and laid them over the fat pieces and the right thigh.
He handed all of this to Aaron and his sons, and they held it up and swung it before Yahweh as a wave offering.
Moses took it back from them and burned it on the altar over the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering. Its smell pleased Yahweh, and it was a gift burned for him.
Moses also took the breast and swung it before Yahweh as a wave offering. It was Moses’ share of the ordination ram, as Yahweh had ordered him.

Moses took a little of the anointing oil and a little of the blood on the altar, and he flicked them over Aaron, his clothes, his sons, and their clothes. That is how Aaron, his sons, and all their clothing were set apart.

Moses said to Aaron and his sons, “Cook the meat by the doorway of the tent of meeting. Eat it there with the bread from the ordination basket, because I was told, ‘Aaron and his sons are to eat it.’{e}
Burn up whatever is left of the meat and bread.
For seven days you must stay away from the tent door, until your ordination period is finished. Over those seven days he will be setting you apart.{f}
Yahweh has ordered everything that was done today, in order to pay for your wrongs.
Stay at the tent’s doorway day and night for seven days and do what Yahweh requires, or you will die. This is the order I received.”
Aaron and his sons carried out all that Yahweh had commanded through Moses.{g}

notes.text: A garment worn by priests over the robe, probably like an apron or a vest, held by shoulder straps and a woven belt (Exodus 28:6-14). Its exact shape is uncertain.
Objects kept in the chest piece and used to learn God’s answer (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21). How they worked is not known.
Hebrew tsits, “flower” or “shining plate,” engraved with the words “Holy to Yahweh” (Exodus 28:36).
Hebrew chitte, “to remove sin” or “to purify.” It comes from the same root as chattat, “sin offering.”
The Hebrew vowels read “as I commanded.” The Septuagint, Syriac, and Targum read “as I was commanded,” as in verse 35.
Literally “for seven days he will fill your hand.” See the note at 7:37.
Literally “by the hand of Moses.”

subheads.1: Setting apart Aaron and his sons

verses.text: On day eight, Moses called together Aaron, Aaron’s sons, and the elders of Israel.
He said to Aaron, “Choose a young bull as your sin offering and a ram as your burnt offering. Neither may have a flaw. Bring them to Yahweh.
Tell the Israelites to choose a male goat for a sin offering. For a burnt offering, tell them to pick a calf and a lamb that are a year old. None may have a flaw.
Choose an ox and a ram as peace offerings to sacrifice before Yahweh, and a grain offering mixed with oil. Today Yahweh will show himself to you.”
The people carried everything Moses had ordered to the front of the meeting tent. The whole community came forward and stood in Yahweh’s presence.
Moses said, “Yahweh gave you these orders so that his glory will show itself to you.”

Then Moses said to Aaron, “Step up to the altar. Present your own sin offering and burnt offering, and pay for your wrongs and for the people’s.{a} After that, present the people’s offerings and pay for their wrongs, just as Yahweh ordered.”
Aaron went up to the altar and killed the calf that was his own sin offering.
His sons handed him the blood. Aaron dipped a finger into it and smeared it on the altar’s horns. What was left he poured out at the foot of the altar.
Aaron burned the fat, the kidneys, and the liver’s best part from the sin offering on the altar, just as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
Outside the camp, he burned the meat and the skin in a fire.
After that he killed the burnt offering. His sons passed him the blood, and he threw it on all sides of the altar.
They gave him the burnt offering in pieces, one after another, along with the head, and he burned each on the altar.
He washed the stomach and legs, then set them on the altar and burned them with the rest of the burnt offering.
Then he brought forward the people’s offering. He took the goat meant as the people’s sin offering, killed it, and offered it for sin the same way he had done the first.
He presented the burnt offering and offered it following the rules.
He presented the grain offering too. He scooped out a handful and burned it on the altar, beside the morning’s burnt offering.
After that he killed the ox and the ram, the people’s peace offering. His sons passed him the blood, and he splashed it on every side of the altar.
The fat parts of the ox and the ram were these: the fat tail, the fat covering the insides, the kidneys, and the liver’s best part.
They laid the fat parts on top of the breasts, and Aaron burned them on the altar.
Aaron held up the breasts and the right thigh and swung them as a wave offering before Yahweh, as Moses had ordered.{b}
Aaron lifted both hands over the people and gave them a blessing.{c} Then he came down from the altar, since the sin offering, the burnt offering, and the peace offerings were done.
Moses and Aaron entered the meeting tent. Coming out again, they blessed the people, and Yahweh’s glory showed itself to everyone.
Fire blazed out from Yahweh and burned up the burnt offering and the fat lying on the altar. The people saw this, gave a loud cry of joy,{d} and dropped face down on the ground.

notes.text: The Septuagint says “for yourself and for your house,” as in 16:6.
Many Hebrew copies, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Septuagint read “as Yahweh had ordered Moses.”
Perhaps with the blessing in Numbers 6:24-26.
Hebrew ranan, a ringing shout, usually of joy.

subheads.1: The first offerings by the priests

verses.text: Aaron’s sons Nadab{a} and Abihu{b} each took a fire pan, filled it with burning coals, and added incense. They offered fire to Yahweh that was not allowed,{c} a thing he had never ordered.
Fire flashed from Yahweh’s presence and burned both of them to death, right there before him.
Moses said to Aaron, “This is what Yahweh meant when he said, ‘I will show that I am holy to those who come near me, and all the people will see my glory.’” Aaron said nothing.
Moses called for Mishael{d} and Elzaphan,{e} sons of Aaron’s uncle Uzziel,{f} and told them, “Come here. Carry your cousins away from the holy place and take them outside the camp.”
They came and lifted the bodies, still in their tunics, and carried them outside the camp, as Moses had said.

Moses then spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar{g} and Ithamar,{h} the sons still alive: “Don’t let your hair go loose{i} and don’t tear your clothes, or you will die, and Yahweh will be angry with everyone. Your relatives, the whole nation of Israel, may mourn for the men Yahweh burned.
Do not even step away from the doorway of the meeting tent, or you will die. Yahweh’s anointing oil is on you.” They did what Moses said.
Yahweh spoke to Aaron and said,
“When you enter the meeting tent, neither you nor your sons may drink wine or any strong drink.{j} Disobey, and you will die. This rule lasts forever, for all your descendants.
You must be able to tell what is holy from what is ordinary, and what is unclean from what is clean.
You must also teach the people of Israel every rule that Yahweh gave them through Moses.”
Moses spoke to Aaron and the sons who were still alive, Eleazar and Ithamar: “Take the grain offering left from Yahweh’s burned gifts, and eat it beside the altar without yeast, for it is most holy.
The place for eating it is a holy one. It is yours and your sons’ portion of Yahweh’s burned gifts, according to my orders.

The breast that was swung, and the thigh that was set apart, may be eaten anywhere that is clean. Your sons and daughters may eat with you. These are your family’s portions from the peace offerings the Israelites bring.

The people must bring the thigh and the breast along with the fat parts that are burned, and swing the breast as a wave offering before Yahweh. It belongs to you and your sons for all time, as Yahweh has ordered.”
Moses looked everywhere for the goat that was the sin offering, only to learn it had been burned. He grew angry at Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s surviving sons, and demanded,
“Why did you leave the sin offering uneaten in the holy place? It is most holy! Yahweh gave it to you to take away the people’s guilt and to pay for their wrongs before him.
Its blood never went inside the holy place, so you were required to eat the meat inside it, just as I commanded.”
Aaron replied, “Today my sons brought a sin offering and a burnt offering to Yahweh, and this is what has happened to me! Would Yahweh have approved if I had eaten the sin offering today?”
Moses heard this and accepted it.{k}

notes.text: Nadab means “generous” or “willing.”
Abihu means “he is my father,” probably meaning God.

Hebrew zarah, “strange” or “foreign.” The text does not say what was wrong with the fire. Some suggest it did not come from the altar (see 16:12), or was offered at the wrong time or place, or that the men were drunk (see verse 9).
Mishael means “who is what God is?”
Elzaphan means “God has protected” or “God has hidden.” He is called Elizaphan in Numbers 3:30.
Uzziel means “God is my strength.”
Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Ithamar may mean “island of palms” or “where is Tamar?” Its meaning is uncertain.
Or “uncover your heads.” Hebrew parah means to let the hair hang loose and untidy, a sign of mourning (13:45; 21:10).
Hebrew shekar, a drink that makes people drunk, perhaps barley beer.

Or “he approved.” The people’s sin offering (9:15) should have been eaten by the priests (6:26). Aaron may mean that after his sons died, the priests were unfit to eat it, or that the deaths had stained the holy place so the offering had to be burned.

verses.text: Yahweh gave these words to Moses and Aaron.
“Tell the people of Israel: Of all the animals on the earth, these are the ones you are allowed to eat.
Any land animal that has a split hoof and also chews the cud is food you may eat.
Some animals chew the cud, or have a split hoof, but not both, and you must not eat them. The camel is one. It chews the cud, yet its hoof is not split, so it is unclean for you.
Another is the rock badger.{a} It chews the cud but its hoof is not split, so it is unclean for you.
Another is the hare.{b} It chews the cud, but its hoof is not split, so it is unclean for you.
Then there is the pig. Its hoof is split, but it never chews the cud, and that makes it unclean for you.
Do not eat their meat, and do not touch their dead bodies. They are unclean for you.
“Of the creatures living in water, you may eat any in the seas or rivers that have fins together with scales.
But every creature in the seas or rivers that has no fins and scales is disgusting{c} to you. That includes the small swarming creatures and any other living thing in the water.
They stay disgusting to you. You must not eat their meat, and you must stay away from their dead bodies.
Anything in the water without fins and scales is disgusting to you.
“You must also treat these birds as disgusting and not eat them: the eagle,{d} the bearded vulture, the black vulture,
the kite, and all kinds of falcons,
all kinds of ravens,
the ostrich,{e} the nighthawk, the seagull, every kind of hawk,
the little owl and the cormorant, the great owl,
the barn owl, then the desert owl, and the carrion vulture,
the stork, each kind of heron, the hoopoe, and the bat.{f}
“Any winged insects that walk on four legs{g} are disgusting to you.
But there are some winged insects with four legs that you may eat: those with jointed legs above their feet, for jumping along the ground.
You may eat any kind of locust, bald locust, cricket, or grasshopper.{h}
Every other winged insect that has four legs is disgusting to you.
“These animals make you unclean. Anyone who touches their dead bodies is unclean until evening.
Anyone who picks up a piece of their carcass must wash his clothes, and he stays unclean until evening.
Animals with a hoof that is not split, or that do not chew the cud, are unclean for you. A person who touches one becomes unclean.
Among the four-footed animals, any that walk on paws are unclean for you. If you touch the body of one after it dies, you are unclean until evening.
Whoever carries one of these bodies must wash his clothes and stays unclean until evening. All these animals are unclean for you.
“Of the little creatures that crawl on the ground, these ones are unclean for you: the mole rat,{i} the mouse, and each kind of large lizard,
the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the sand lizard, and also the chameleon.
Of all the crawling animals, these are unclean for you. Anyone who touches one when it is dead is unclean until evening.

Whatever one of them falls on after it dies becomes unclean. That includes wooden tools, clothes, leather, and sacks, and anything else used for work. Put it in water. It stays unclean until evening, and then it is clean.
If one of them drops into a clay pot, everything inside the pot becomes unclean, and you must smash the pot.
Any food in it that could be eaten becomes unclean if water from that pot touches it. Any drink from such a pot is unclean too.
Whatever a dead body falls on is unclean. If it lands on an oven or a stove,{j} that must be broken to pieces. These things are unclean, and you must treat them as unclean from then on.
A spring or a cistern that holds water stays clean, but a person who touches the dead body in it is unclean.
If part of a dead body falls on seed that is meant for planting, the seed is still clean.
But if the seed has been soaked in water and then part of a dead body falls on it, the seed is unclean for you.
“If an animal that you are allowed to eat dies on its own, anyone who touches its dead body is unclean until evening.
A person who eats some of its meat must wash his clothes and stays unclean until evening. A person who carries its body must also wash his clothes and stays unclean until evening.
“Every small creature that crawls on the ground is disgusting. Do not eat it.
This includes anything that moves on its belly, on four legs, or on many feet, among all the creatures that crawl on the ground. Do not eat them, because they are disgusting.
Do not make yourselves disgusting by eating any crawling creature. Do not make yourselves unclean or stained by them.
I am Yahweh your God. Make yourselves holy, because I am holy.{k} Do not stain yourselves with any creature that crawls on the ground.
It was I, Yahweh, who brought you up from Egypt so that I would be your God. You belong to a holy God, so be holy yourselves.”
These are the teachings about animals, birds, every living thing in the water, and every creature that crawls on the ground.
They teach you to tell the unclean from the clean, and the animals you may eat from the ones you may not.

notes.text: Hebrew shaphan, probably the rock hyrax, a small animal that lives among rocks (Psalm 104:18; Proverbs 30:26).

The hyrax and the hare do not really chew the cud as cattle do. But their jaws keep moving, and they eat their own soft droppings again, so they look as if they do. The law goes by what people can see, not by modern animal science. The Septuagint names these two animals differently.
Hebrew sheqets, a stronger word than “unclean.” It is used for things to be avoided with disgust.
Hebrew nesher, which may include the griffon vulture. Many bird names in verses 13-19 cannot be known for certain. The names here are the traditional or likely ones.
Or “eagle owl.” Hebrew bath hayaanah, literally “daughter of the desert” or “daughter of greed.”
The bat is listed with birds because it flies. Hebrew oph means any winged creature.
That is, insects. They seem to move on four legs when they walk.
The four Hebrew names are arbeh, salam, chargol, and chagav. All are kinds of locust or grasshopper, but exactly which is uncertain.
Hebrew choled, traditionally “weasel,” but probably the mole rat. The animals in verses 29-30 are not identified for certain.
Hebrew kirayim, found only here. It was probably a stove with two parts.
This command is repeated in 11:45, 19:2, and 20:26. It is the main theme of Leviticus, and it is quoted in 1 Peter 1:16.

subheads.39: Animals that die on their own

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: A woman who becomes pregnant{a} and has a baby boy is unclean for seven days, as she is at the time of her monthly period.{b}
A boy is to be circumcised when he is eight days old.
She then stays at home thirty-three more days while her bleeding is cleansed. Until those days are finished, she may not touch any holy thing, and she may not go into the sanctuary.
If the baby is a girl, the woman is unclean for fourteen days, like her time of monthly bleeding. Then sixty-six more days must pass while she is being cleansed from her bleeding.{c}

“When the days of her cleansing are over, for a son or a daughter, she brings two gifts to the priest at the meeting tent’s doorway: a one-year-old lamb to be burned whole, and a young pigeon or dove as a sin offering.

The priest offers them in front of Yahweh and makes her right with him, and the flow of her blood no longer makes her unclean. That is the teaching for any woman who has a baby, whether a boy or a girl.
A woman too poor for a lamb can bring two doves or two young pigeons, one to be burned whole and the other for the sin offering. The priest makes her right with Yahweh, and she is clean.”{d}

notes.text: Hebrew tazria, literally “produces seed,” meaning she becomes pregnant.
Hebrew niddah, the time set apart during a woman’s period (15:19-24).

The text does not say why the time is doubled for a girl. This uncleanness was about ceremony, not about wrongdoing. Having a baby is not a sin (see the blessing in Genesis 1:28). The sin offering here is better understood as a cleansing offering (see the note at 4:3).
Mary brought the offering for poor families after Jesus was born (Luke 2:22-24).

subheads.6: The gift for being clean again

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron and said,

“Suppose someone gets a swelling, a crusty patch, or a shiny spot on his skin, and it may turn into an unclean skin disease.{a} He must be taken to Aaron the priest or to one of Aaron’s sons who are priests.

The priest looks at the sore{b} on his skin. If the hair there has turned white and the place seems deeper than the rest of his skin, then it is an unclean skin disease. After examining the man, the priest declares him unclean.
But suppose the spot is white yet looks level with the skin, and the hair in it is still dark. In that case the priest shuts the sick person away for seven days.
On day seven, the priest checks him again. If the sore looks the same and has not spread across his skin, the priest keeps him apart for seven more days.
On day seven again, the priest looks once more. If the sore has faded and has not spread, the priest declares him clean. It was only a crusty patch. The man washes his clothes, and he is clean.
But if the patch spreads on his skin after the priest has declared him clean, he must go to the priest again.
The priest checks him, and if the patch has spread, the priest declares him unclean. It is an unclean skin disease.
“Whenever someone has an unclean skin disease, he is to be brought to the priest.
The priest checks him. Perhaps there is a white swelling on the skin, the hair there is white, and raw flesh shows inside the swelling.
the disease has settled into his body. The priest declares him unclean. He does not need to keep him apart, since the man is already unclean.
Now suppose the disease breaks out all over the skin and covers the sick person from head to foot, as far as the priest can see.
The priest checks him, and if the disease covers his whole body, he declares the sick person clean.{c} All of him has turned white, so he is clean.
But any time raw flesh shows on him, he is unclean.
When the priest sees raw flesh, he declares him unclean. Raw flesh is unclean. It is an unclean skin disease.
Should the raw flesh change and turn white, he returns to the priest.
The priest checks him. If the sore has turned white, the priest declares the sick person clean, and he is clean.
“Suppose a boil appears on someone’s skin and then heals,
and in its place a white swelling or a reddish-white shiny spot appears. He must show it to the priest.
The priest looks at it. If it seems sunken below the skin and its hair has turned white, the priest declares him unclean. It is an unclean skin disease that broke out in the boil.
But if the priest looks and sees no white hair in it, and it is not sunken but has faded, the priest keeps him apart for seven days.
If the patch keeps spreading over the skin, the priest declares him unclean, because it is a disease.
If the spot never moves from its place and does not grow, it is just the scar from the boil. The priest declares the man clean.
“Suppose someone has a burn on his skin, and the raw place turns into a shiny spot, reddish-white or white.

The priest looks at it. If the hair in the shiny spot has turned white and the spot seems deeper than the skin, it is an unclean skin disease that broke out in the burn. The priest declares him unclean.
But if the priest looks and finds no white hair in the spot, and it is not sunken but has faded, the priest keeps him apart for seven days.
On day seven the priest checks him. If it has spread on the skin, the priest declares him unclean. It is an unclean skin disease.
If the spot has stayed in place, has not grown, and has faded, it is only a swelling left by the burn. The scar is all it is, so the priest declares the man clean.
“Take a man or a woman who has a sore on the head or on the chin.

the priest examines it. If it seems deeper than the skin and the hair in it is yellow and thin, the priest declares that person unclean. It is a scaly sore,{d} an unclean skin disease on the head or chin.
But if the priest looks at the scaly sore and sees that it is not deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, he keeps the person apart for seven days.
On day seven the priest examines the sore. If it has not spread, no yellow hair is in it, and it does not look deeper than the skin,
the person shaves, but leaves the sore itself unshaved. The priest then keeps him apart for seven more days.
On day seven the priest looks at the sore again. If it has not grown larger and seems level with the skin, the priest declares the person clean. After washing his clothes he is clean.
Suppose, however, the sore starts spreading on his skin once he has been declared clean.
the priest examines him. The sore has grown larger on the skin, so the priest need not search for yellow hair. The man is unclean.
If, in the priest’s view, the sore has stayed the same and black hair is growing there, it has healed. The man is clean, and the priest says so.
“Suppose a man or woman has shiny spots on the skin, and the spots are white.
The priest looks, and if the spots are a dull white, it is only a harmless rash{e} that broke out on the skin. The person is clean.
“A man who has lost the hair from his head is bald, yet he is clean.
When hair falls from the front of his head, he has a high forehead, yet he is clean.
But suppose a reddish-white sore appears on the bald head or forehead. It is an unclean skin disease breaking out there.
The priest examines him. If the swollen sore on his bald head or forehead is reddish-white, like an unclean skin disease on other skin,
the man has an unclean skin disease. He is unclean, and the priest must declare him so. The sore is on his head.
“Anyone with an unclean skin disease must wear ripped clothes, let his hair hang loose, and cover his mustache.{f} Wherever he goes, he calls out, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’
He stays unclean for the whole time he has the disease. Because he is unclean, he must live by himself, with his home outside the camp.
“Suppose an unclean mold{g} appears on a piece of clothing, either woolen or linen,
on the threads,{h} lengthwise or crosswise, in linen or wool, or on leather or any leather goods,
If the spot on the cloth or leather, or on the threads, or on anything leather, is greenish or reddish, it is an unclean mold, and it must be shown to the priest.
The priest looks at the spot and locks the item away for seven days.
On day seven he checks it. If the spot has spread across the clothing, the threads, or the leather, whatever it is used for, the mold is harmful.{i} The item is unclean.
He must burn the clothing, the threads, the wool, the linen, or the leather item that has the mold. It is harmful mold, so it must be burned in fire.
But if the priest looks and the spot has not spread across the clothing, the threads, or the leather,
he orders the item to be washed, and he locks it away for seven more days.
After the washing, the priest looks at it again. If the spot looks the same, even though it did not grow, the item is unclean. Burn it up, whether the rot is on the front or the back.{j}
If the priest looks and the spot has faded after washing, he tears that piece out of the clothing, leather, or threads.
But if the spot appears again on the clothing, threads, or leather, it is breaking out again. Burn the item in fire.
Clothing, threads, or leather items that lose the spot after being washed must be washed one more time, and then they are clean.”
This is the rule for an unclean mold on clothing made of wool or linen, on threads, or on any leather item. It tells how to declare each one clean or unclean.

notes.text: Hebrew tsaraat, usually translated “leprosy.” But it is not Hansen’s disease, which is what we now call leprosy. The signs listed here do not fit that illness, and the same word is used for growths on cloth, leather, and house walls (13:47-59; 14:33-53). It covers many scaly or flaking skin conditions, such as psoriasis, vitiligo, and fungus infections. Here it is translated “unclean skin disease” for people, and “unclean mold” for cloth and houses.
Hebrew nega, literally “a touch” or “a blow,” meaning a mark or sore. People often thought of such sores as sent by God (see 14:34).
The whitening of the whole body apparently showed that the illness had finished and was no longer active.
Hebrew netheq, from a verb that may mean “to tear off.” It was a condition of the scalp or beard, maybe ringworm or scaly eczema.
Hebrew bohaq, found only here. It may have been a harmless white rash, such as vitiligo.
Or “upper lip.” Covering the mouth area was a sign of mourning (Ezekiel 24:17, 22; Micah 3:7).
Hebrew tsaraat, the same word as for the skin disease (see the note at verse 2). On cloth and leather, it probably means mold, mildew, or fungus.
Or possibly “in the woven or knitted material.” The exact meaning of the Hebrew words shethi and erev is uncertain.
Hebrew mamereth, “harmful” or “painful,” a word found only in 13:51-52 and 14:44.
Literally “whether in its bald back or its bald front,” meaning the worn spots on the inside or outside of the cloth. The Hebrew is uncertain.
