subheads.9: A disease that has lasted a long time
subheads.29: Sores on the head or chin

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“These are the instructions for a person who had an unclean skin disease and is ready to be made clean. He is brought to the priest.
The priest goes outside the camp to meet him and looks him over. If the sickness has gone from his skin,
the priest has two living clean birds brought for the man who is being cleansed. He also asks for cedar wood, red yarn, and a hyssop branch.{a}
Then the priest orders one bird to be killed over fresh water in a clay bowl.{b}
He picks up the living bird together with the cedar, the red yarn, and the hyssop, and dips all of it into the blood of the dead bird, which was killed above the fresh water.
Seven times he sprinkles the blood on the man who is being cleansed from the disease. Then he declares him clean and lets the living bird fly away over the open countryside.
The man washes his clothes, shaves off every hair, and bathes in water. Then he is clean. He may now enter the camp, but for seven days he must stay outside his own tent.
On day seven he shaves off all his hair again, including his head, beard, and eyebrows, every bit of it. He washes his clothes and bathes in water, and he is clean.

“On day eight he brings two male lambs with nothing wrong with them, along with a one-year-old female lamb that is also perfect. He also needs a grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, six quarts of it,{c} and a small measure of oil, about a third of a quart.{d}
The priest who is making him clean stands him at the doorway of the meeting tent in front of Yahweh, together with all these gifts.
The priest takes one of the male lambs and presents it as a guilt offering, along with the measure of oil,{e} lifting them up as a wave offering to Yahweh.
He kills the lamb in the holy area, at the spot used for killing sin offerings and burnt offerings. The guilt offering belongs to the priest, as the sin offering does, and it is most holy.
The priest takes some of the guilt offering’s blood and touches it to the bottom of the right ear of the man being cleansed, then to his right thumb, and then to the big toe of his right foot.
Next the priest pours some of the oil into his own left palm.
With a finger of his right hand, he dips into the oil that is in his left palm, and flicks some of it seven times toward Yahweh.
From the oil still in his hand, the priest puts some on the same three places: the man’s right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe. He puts it over the blood of the guilt offering.
Whatever oil is left in his hand, the priest rubs on the man’s head. So the priest makes him right with Yahweh.
Then the priest offers the sin offering to cleanse the man from his uncleanness, and afterward he kills the burnt offering.
The priest sets the grain offering and the burnt offering on the altar and makes the man right with Yahweh. Now he is clean.

“If the man is poor and cannot pay for all that, he brings only one male lamb as a guilt offering to be lifted up, so that he may be made right. For the grain offering he also needs fine flour mixed with oil, two quarts of it,{f} and the same third of a quart of oil.
He adds two doves or two young pigeons, whichever he can pay for. The first is for a sin offering, and the second is for a burnt offering.
On day eight he brings them to the priest for his cleansing, at the doorway of the meeting tent in front of Yahweh.
The priest takes the guilt offering lamb and the oil and lifts them up in front of Yahweh.
He kills the lamb of the guilt offering, takes some of its blood, and puts it on the man’s right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe.
The priest pours some of the oil into his own left hand
and flicks oil from his left hand with a finger of his right seven times toward Yahweh.
Then he dabs oil from his hand on the same places, the man’s right ear, right thumb, and right big toe, right over the spots of blood.
The oil left in his hand he puts on the head of the man being cleansed, to make him right with Yahweh.
After that, he offers the doves or young pigeons the man could pay for,
One bird is the sin offering and the other the burnt offering, and the grain offering goes with them. So the priest makes the man right with Yahweh.{g}
These are the instructions for a person with an unclean skin disease who cannot pay the usual price for being made clean.”
Yahweh addressed Moses and Aaron:
“After you enter Canaan,{h} the land I am giving you to own, I may cause an unclean mold to appear in a house in your land.
The owner of that house must go and tell the priest, ‘I think I see something like a mold in my house.’
Before going in to look at it, the priest orders the house emptied, so nothing inside becomes unclean. Then the priest goes in to inspect it.
He looks at the spots on the walls. If they are greenish or reddish dips{i} that seem to go below the surface of the wall,
the priest walks out to the front door and shuts the house up for seven days.
On day seven he comes back to look. If the spots have crept further across the walls,
he orders the affected stones pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the town.
He has the whole inside of the house scraped, and the scraped plaster is thrown away in an unclean spot outside the town.
They set other stones where the old ones were, and the house is plastered again with fresh plaster.
“Suppose the mold returns and breaks out again in the house after the stones were removed and the walls scraped and replastered.
The priest goes to look. If the mold has spread, it is harmful mold in the house, and the house is unclean.
It must be torn down, with its stones, wood, and plaster, and all of it carried out to an unclean place outside the town.
Whoever goes into the house during the days it is shut up is unclean until the sun goes down.
Anyone who lies down or eats there has to wash his clothes.
“But suppose the priest returns and sees that the mold did not spread after the replastering. He declares the house clean, because the mold is gone.
To make the house clean, he takes two birds, cedar wood, red yarn, and a hyssop branch.
He kills one bird over fresh water in a clay bowl.
Then he takes the cedar, hyssop, red yarn, and the living bird, dips them into the dead bird’s blood and the fresh water, and sprinkles the house seven times.
So he cleans the house using the blood of the bird, fresh water, the living bird, cedar, hyssop, and the red yarn.
He lets the living bird fly off into the open countryside outside the town. That is how he makes the house right, and it is clean.”
These are the instructions for every kind of unclean skin disease, including scaly sores,
mold in clothing or in a house,
a swelling, a crusty patch, or a shiny spot.
They show when something is unclean and when it is clean. These are the teachings about such diseases.

notes.text: Hebrew ezov, probably Syrian hyssop or marjoram (Origanum syriacum). Its bushy stems could be used for sprinkling (Exodus 12:22; Psalm 51:7).
Literally “living water,” meaning fresh water from a spring or stream, not standing water.
Hebrew “three-tenths of an ephah,” about 6.6 liters (6 quarts). Ancient measures varied.

Hebrew “one log,” a liquid measure used in the Bible only in this chapter (14:10, 12, 15, 21, 24). Later Jewish writings make it about a twelfth of a hin, roughly 0.3 liter. The ancient size is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads kotyle, “a small cup.”
Hebrew “with the log of oil,” also in verses 15 and 24. This is the oil measured out in verse 10.
Hebrew “one-tenth of an ephah,” about 2.2 liters (2 quarts).
The Greek Old Testament leaves out “whatever he can pay for” at the start of this verse. The Hebrew repeats the phrase from verse 30, and this translation does not repeat it.
The meaning of the name Canaan is uncertain. It may be related to a word for purple dye (compare Genesis 9:18).
Hebrew shequaruroth, a word found only here. It may mean “dips” or “streaks.”

subheads.1: Cleansing a person who has been healed
subheads.21: The offering of a poor person

verses.text: Yahweh addressed Moses and Aaron:
“Tell the Israelites: When a man has a flow coming from his body,{a} that flow is unclean.
Whether the flow keeps running or is stopped up, the man is unclean.{b}
Any bed he lies on is unclean, and so is anything he sits on.
If you touch his bed, you must wash your clothes, bathe in water, and stay unclean until evening.
If you sit where he sat, you must wash your clothes, bathe, and stay unclean until evening.
Touching his body means washing your clothes and bathing in water, and you stay unclean until evening.
If he spits on a clean person, that person washes his clothes, bathes, and is unclean until evening.
Any saddle the man rides on is unclean.
Whoever touches something that was under him is unclean until evening. A person who carries such things must wash his clothes, bathe, and remain unclean until evening.
If the man touches someone without first rinsing his hands, that person washes his clothes, bathes in water, and is unclean until evening.
A clay pot he touches must be smashed, and any wooden item he touches must be rinsed with water.
“When the man’s flow stops, he counts seven days for being cleansed. Then he washes his clothes and bathes in fresh running water, and he is clean.
On day eight he takes two doves or two young pigeons, goes in front of Yahweh to the doorway of the meeting tent, and hands them to the priest.
The priest offers one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. In this way the priest makes the man right with Yahweh for his flow.
“A man who has a release of semen must bathe his entire body in water. He is unclean until evening.
Any cloth or leather with semen on it has to be washed with water, and it stays unclean until evening.
If a man and woman sleep together and he releases semen, both must bathe in water, and both are unclean until evening.
“A woman who has blood flowing from her body has her monthly period. For seven days she is unclean, and whoever touches her stays unclean until the sun sets.
Whatever she lies on during her period is unclean, and so is whatever she sits on.
Whoever touches her bed has to wash his clothes and bathe, and he is unclean until evening.
Whoever touches a seat she used has to wash his clothes and bathe, and he is unclean until evening.
Be it the bed or a seat she used, whoever touches it is unclean until the sun sets.
If a man sleeps with her and her period begins while they are together, he is unclean for a week. Every bed he lies on is unclean too.
“A woman may bleed for many days when it is not the time of her period, or her period may last longer than usual. All the days of this unclean flow, she is unclean, just as during her period.{c}
Every bed she lies on while her flow lasts is treated as her bed is during her period. Whatever she sits on is unclean, as it is then.
Anyone who touches these things is unclean. He washes his clothes and bathes, and he is unclean until the sun goes down.
When her flow stops, she counts seven days, and then she is clean.
On day eight she takes two doves or two young pigeons and brings them to the priest at the doorway of the meeting tent.
The priest offers one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. So the priest makes her right with Yahweh for her unclean flow.
“You are to keep the Israelites apart from what makes them unclean. Otherwise they will die in their uncleanness, for making my tent of worship in their midst unclean.”
These are the instructions for a man with a flow, for a man made unclean by a release of semen,
for a woman who is unwell with her period, for any man or woman with a flow, and for a man who sleeps with an unclean woman.

notes.text: Literally “from his flesh,” a polite way to refer to his private parts. The flow is probably a sickness, such as gonorrhea or another infection, and not a normal release (verse 16).

The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Greek Old Testament, and a Dead Sea Scroll of Leviticus (11QpaleoLev-a) add: “all the days of the flow from his body, whether his body runs with the flow or is blocked by it.” A scribe’s eye may have skipped between the similar phrases in the standard Hebrew text.
Compare the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years (Mark 5:25-34).

subheads.1: A man with a bodily discharge

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses after the two sons of Aaron died, when they came too close to Yahweh.{a}

Yahweh said to Moses, “Warn your brother Aaron that he may not walk behind the curtain into the holy place whenever he pleases. The cover{b} on the ark is there, and I appear in a cloud over it. If Aaron comes carelessly, he will die.
Here is how Aaron may enter the holy place: he brings a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering.

He puts on the holy linen shirt, wears linen shorts against his body, ties on the linen sash, and wraps his head in the linen turban. Since these clothes are holy, he first washes his whole body in water, and only then dresses.
From Israel’s community he receives two male goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.
“Aaron first offers the bull as a sin offering for himself, and so makes things right for himself and his family.
Then he takes the two goats and stands them in front of Yahweh at the doorway of the meeting tent.
He throws lots for the two goats. One lot is marked for Yahweh, and the other for Azazel.{c}
Aaron leads forward the goat on which Yahweh’s lot fell and offers it as a sin offering.
The other goat, the one picked for Azazel, is kept alive in front of Yahweh. Over it he makes things right,{d} and then it is sent into the wilderness to Azazel.
“Aaron brings the bull that is the sin offering for himself, and he makes things right for himself and his family. He kills his bull as the sin offering.
He takes a pan full of burning coals from the altar in front of Yahweh, and two handfuls of fine sweet incense, and carries them behind the curtain.
There, in front of Yahweh, he puts the incense on the fire. Its cloud covers the lid over the ark’s tablets,{e} so that he does not die.
He takes some of the bull’s blood and, with a finger, sprinkles it across the front of the cover.{f} Facing the cover, he then flicks blood from his finger seven times.
“Next he kills the goat of the sin offering for the people and carries its blood past the curtain. This blood gets the same treatment as the bull’s: he sprinkles it over the cover and in front of it.

So he makes the holy place right, because of the Israelites’ uncleanness, their rebellion, and all their sins. He does the same for the meeting tent, which stands among them in the middle of their uncleanness.

No one else may be inside the meeting tent while Aaron is in the holy place making things right, until he walks out. By then he has paid for his own sins, his family’s, and those of the entire community of Israel.
After that he goes out to the altar in front of Yahweh and makes it right. He takes some bull’s blood and some goat’s blood and puts it on all the horns of the altar.
With his finger he sprinkles some blood on it seven times. In this way he cleans it and sets it apart, away from the uncleanness of the Israelites.
“Once Aaron has made the holy place, the meeting tent, and the altar right, he brings forward the living goat.

He rests both hands on its head and confesses over it all the wrongs of the Israelites, all their rebellion and every sin. He lays them on the goat’s head. Then a man chosen for the job leads it away into the wilderness.{g}
The goat carries all their wrongs on itself to a faraway land,{h} where the man turns it loose in the wilderness.
“Aaron then goes into the meeting tent, takes off the linen clothes he put on to enter the holy place, and leaves them there.
He bathes in water in a holy place, puts on his usual clothes, and comes out. He offers his own burnt offering and the people’s burnt offering, and makes things right for himself and for the people.
Aaron also burns the sin offering’s fat on the altar.
Whoever took the goat out to Azazel washes his clothes and bathes in water. After this he is allowed back in the camp.
The bull and the goat of the sin offering, whose blood went into the holy place, are carried outside the camp. Their skins, meat, and waste are burned in a fire.
The man who burns them washes his clothes and bathes in water. After that he is back in good standing and may go into the camp.

“This is a rule for you for all time. Every year, on the tenth day of the seventh month (September-October),{i} you must humble yourselves{j} and do no work. This is true for native-born Israelites and for foreigners living among you.
On that day things are made right for you so that you become clean. In Yahweh’s sight you are clean of every sin.
It is a day of total rest,{k} and you must humble yourselves. This is a rule for all time.
The priest who is anointed and appointed to follow his father as priest does the ceremony. He wears the holy linen clothes.
He makes the holy place{l} right, then the meeting tent and the altar, and last the priests and the entire gathered people.
You must keep this rule for all time: once every year, things are made right for the Israelites because of all their sins.” Moses did just as Yahweh ordered him.{m}

notes.text: The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek Old Testament read “when they offered strange fire in front of Yahweh and died,” which recalls 10:1-2.

Hebrew kapporet, from the same root as kipper, “to make right” or “to cover.” It is traditionally called the “mercy seat,” a name that came through William Tyndale from the German of Martin Luther. See the note at Exodus 25:17.

Hebrew laazazel, “for Azazel,” a word found only in this chapter (verses 8, 10, 26). Its meaning is much debated. (1) It may be a name, perhaps of a wilderness demon, matching “for Yahweh” in the same verse. The book of 1 Enoch (chapters 8-10) makes Azazel the leader of fallen angels. (2) It may mean “the goat that goes away,” from ez, “goat,” and azal, “go away.” That is where the old English word “scapegoat” comes from. (3) It may be a place, “a rugged cliff” or “a steep drop,” as some Jewish teachers thought. (4) It may be an abstract word meaning “complete removal.” The name is kept here as it stands in the Hebrew. In none of these readings is the goat a sacrifice offered to Azazel. It carries Israel’s sins away (verses 21-22).
Or “makes things right with it,” or “performs cleansing over it.” The exact sense of kipper here is debated, since this goat is not killed.
The stone tablets of the covenant inside the ark (Exodus 25:16, 21).
Literally “on the face of the cover toward the east.”
Hebrew itti, a word found only here. It may mean “appointed” or “standing ready.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a man ready at hand.”
Hebrew gezerah, literally “cut off,” a land from which there is no return.

Hebrew “the seventh month,” counted from the spring start of Israel’s religious year (Exodus 12:2). The months followed the moon, so the seventh month (later called Tishri) fell in September-October. This tenth day became Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement (23:26-32).
Literally “afflict your souls.” Jewish tradition understood this as fasting and other self-denial (compare Psalm 35:13; Isaiah 58:3, 5; Acts 27:9, “the Fast”).
Hebrew shabbat shabbaton, a rest of the highest degree.
Literally “the holy sanctuary.”

Hebrew “and he did,” meaning that Aaron carried out these instructions when the day came. The Greek Old Testament reads “it shall be done once in the year, as the Lord commanded Moses.” Hebrews 9:6-14, 24-28 explains this day in light of Christ.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell Aaron, his sons, and all the Israelites that Yahweh has given this order:
“Any Israelite who kills an ox, lamb, or goat, in the camp or somewhere outside it,
and never brings it to the front of the meeting tent{a} as a gift for Yahweh in front of Yahweh’s dwelling, is guilty of bloodshed. He has spilled blood, and his people will cut him off.

The purpose is that Israelites bring Yahweh the animals they now kill out in the open fields. At the entrance of the meeting tent they hand them to the priest, who offers them to Yahweh as peace offerings.
The priest throws the blood on Yahweh’s altar at the doorway of the meeting tent and burns the fat, a smell that pleases Yahweh.
Then the people will no longer offer their animals to the goat spirits,{b} chasing after them like unfaithful lovers. This is a rule for them and their descendants for all time.
“Say to them as well: If any Israelite, or any foreigner who lives among them, offers a burnt offering or other sacrifice
and does not take it there for Yahweh, that person will be removed from his people.
“Any Israelite, or foreigner living among them, who eats blood will have me against him. I will remove that person from his people.
The life{c} in a body is in the blood. I gave you the blood for the altar, to make you right with me. It is the life inside the blood that does this.{d}
This is why I told the Israelites, ‘None of you may eat blood, and neither may any foreigner who lives with you.’
Any Israelite or foreigner among them who hunts down a wild animal or a bird that can be eaten must pour out its blood and cover it with dirt.

The life of any creature is the blood in it.{e} That is why I told the Israelites, ‘Never eat the blood of any creature, for every creature’s life is its blood, and anyone who eats it will be cut off.’
“Anyone, native-born or foreign, who eats an animal that died by itself or was torn apart by wild animals must wash his clothes and bathe in water. He is unclean until evening, and then he is clean.
If he does not wash his clothes and bathe, he must pay for his wrong.”

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and a Dead Sea Scroll of Leviticus (4QLev-d) add here: “to make it a burnt offering or a peace offering to Yahweh, to be accepted as a pleasing smell, and kills it outside, and does not bring it to the doorway of the meeting tent.” Another scroll, 11QpaleoLev-a, has the shorter text of the standard Hebrew, which is followed here.

Hebrew seirim, literally “hairy ones” or “goats.” These were goat-like spirits or idols thought to live in the wilderness (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14; 2 Chronicles 11:15). The Greek Old Testament reads “vain things,” meaning idols.
Hebrew nephesh, “soul,” “life,” or “person.” It is used this way throughout verses 11-14.
Or “makes things right for the life” or “as a life” (in place of the life). The Hebrew bannephesh can mean “by means of the life” or “in exchange for the life.” Compare Hebrews 9:22.
The Hebrew of this phrase is hard to read. Literally it says “its blood is in its life.”

subheads.1: Sacrifices must be brought to the tent

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: I am Yahweh your God.
Do not copy the ways of Egypt, where you used to live, or the ways of Canaan, where I am bringing you. Do not live by their customs.
Obey my laws and follow my rules, and live by them. I am Yahweh your God.
Keep my rules and laws, because the one who follows them will live through them.{a} I am Yahweh.
“None of you may go near a close relative{b} for sex.{c} I am Yahweh.
Never dishonor your father by sleeping with your mother. She is your own mother, so she is off limits to you.
Your father’s wife is also off limits. Sleeping with her would dishonor your father himself.
A sister is not to be touched this way, born to your father or to your mother, raised in your home or in another.
Stay away from your granddaughter, the daughter of your son or of your daughter. Her shame would be your own.
A half sister, the daughter of your father’s wife who was born to your father, is also your sister. Leave her alone.
Do not sleep with your father’s sister, since she is a close relative of your father.
Likewise your mother’s sister is too close, because she is your mother’s relative by blood.
Do not dishonor your father’s brother by approaching his wife. She is your aunt.
Your daughter-in-law is your son’s wife, and you may never sleep with her.
Your brother’s wife belongs to him, and sleeping with her would shame your brother.{d}

Never sleep with a woman and then with her daughter as well. And do not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter for such a purpose. They are close relatives, and it is a shameful wickedness.{e}
Never marry a woman as a rival to her own sister, and sleep with her while the sister is alive.{f}
“Do not go near a woman to have sex with her while she is unclean during her monthly period.
Do not sleep with your neighbor’s wife, which would make you unclean.
Do not give any of your children to be passed over{g} to Molech,{h} for that would dishonor the name of your God. I am Yahweh.
You must not lie with a man the way you would lie with a woman. It is detestable.{i}
Never have sex with an animal, which would make you unclean. A woman likewise must never present herself to an animal to mate with it. That is a twisted act.{j}
“Keep yourselves from becoming unclean through any of this. The nations I am driving out ahead of you made themselves unclean through every one of these acts.
Even the land became unclean. So I punished it for its wrongdoing, and the land threw out the people living in it.
You, however, must keep my rules and laws. None of these detestable acts may be done by anyone born here or by a foreigner living among you,
(the people who lived in this land before you did every one of them, and the land became unclean),{k}
If you spoil the land that way, it will spit you out, as it spat out the nation that lived there before.
Whoever commits any of these detestable acts will lose his place among his people.
Obey my orders, and do not follow the detestable customs that people practiced before you came. Do not make yourselves unclean by them. I am Yahweh your God.”

notes.text: Quoted in Nehemiah 9:29; Ezekiel 20:11; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12.
Literally “flesh of his flesh.”

“Uncover nakedness” is a Hebrew way of speaking about sexual relations. The same idiom is used all through this chapter, and this translation says “sleep with,” “go near,” or “shame” depending on the verse.
Compare the duty of marrying a dead brother’s widow in Deuteronomy 25:5-10, which applies when the brother died without a son.
Hebrew zimmah, a deliberate, shameful wickedness.
The Hebrew can also be read as banning a second wife in general (“a woman in addition to another”), which is how the Damascus Document of Qumran understood it. But the usual meaning is a sister.
Hebrew lehaavir, “to make pass over.” It is often understood as passing children through fire (2 Kings 23:10), meaning child sacrifice. The Greek Old Testament reads “to serve a ruler.”

Hebrew molek, probably a god to whom children were sacrificed, though some scholars take it as the name of a kind of sacrifice. The vowels may be those of bosheth, “shame,” added to the consonants of melek, “king.” The Greek Old Testament here reads archon, “ruler,” and in 20:2 it reads Moloch.
Hebrew toevah, something hateful or abhorrent. The same word is used in verses 26-30.
Hebrew tevel, “confusion,” a mixing of what should be kept apart.
A Dead Sea Scroll of Leviticus (11QpaleoLev-a) sets this verse off with marks like parentheses, as this translation does too.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the whole community of the Israelites: Be holy. I, Yahweh your God, am holy.{a}
Honor your mother and your father, each one of you, and keep my Sabbaths. I am Yahweh your God.
Do not turn toward worthless idols{b} or cast metal gods for yourselves. I am Yahweh your God.
“When you bring a peace offering to Yahweh, offer it in a way that he will accept.
You may eat it on the day you offer it or on the next day, but whatever is left on the third day must be burned.
Anyone who eats any of it on the third day has eaten something foul,{c} and the offering will not be accepted.
He will answer for his wrong, since he treated what is holy to Yahweh like something common. His people will cut that person off.
“When you harvest your land’s crops, do not cut the grain right to the edges of your field, and do not go back to pick up what you missed.
Do not strip your vineyard bare or pick up the grapes that fall. Leave them for the poor and for foreigners. I am Yahweh your God.
“Do not steal. Do not cheat or lie to each other.
Do not make a false promise using my name, which would dishonor the name of your God. I am Yahweh.
“Do not take advantage of your neighbor or rob him. Never keep a hired worker’s pay overnight until morning.
Do not insult a deaf person or put something in a blind person’s way to trip him. Show respect for your God. I am Yahweh.
“Do not twist justice when you judge. Do not favor the poor, and do not give special treatment to the powerful. Judge your neighbor fairly.
Do not spread lies about others among your people. Do not stand by while your neighbor’s life{d} is in danger. I am Yahweh.
“Do not hold hatred for your relative in your heart. Speak honestly to your neighbor about what he has done wrong, so that you do not share his guilt.{e}
Do not take revenge, and do not carry a grudge against any of your people. Care for your neighbor as much as you care for yourself.{f} I am Yahweh.
“Keep my rules. Do not cross-breed your animals. Do not scatter two kinds of seed in a field. Do not put on clothes made from two kinds of cloth.{g}
“A man may sleep with a slave woman engaged to another man,{h} yet she has not been bought back or freed. A penalty must follow.{i} Neither of them is to die, since she was not free.
To make this right, the man brings a ram to Yahweh at the meeting tent’s doorway as a guilt offering.
The priest makes him right with Yahweh by offering the guilt offering ram for the sin he committed, and the sin is forgiven.
“When you enter the land and plant fruit trees, consider the fruit off limits.{j} For three years you may not eat it.
In the fourth year all of the fruit is holy, a gift of praise to Yahweh.
When the fifth year comes, you may eat its fruit. In this way the trees will yield even more for you. I am Yahweh your God.
“Never eat meat that still has blood in it.{k} Do not practice fortune-telling or magic.{l}
Do not trim the hair at the sides of your head or cut the edges of your beard.
Do not slash your body when you mourn the dead, and do not tattoo yourselves. I am Yahweh.
Do not dishonor your daughter by making her a prostitute. Otherwise the land will turn to prostitution and fill up with evil.
Keep my Sabbaths and show respect for my holy place. I am Yahweh.
“Do not turn to mediums or those who consult spirits.{m} Do not go looking for them, or they will make you unclean. I am Yahweh your God.
“Stand up when an older person with gray hair enters the room, and show respect to the elderly. Honor your God. I am Yahweh.
“If a foreigner settles with you in your country, you must not mistreat him.
Treat the foreigner as one of your own people, and love him as you love yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
“Do not cheat when you judge, or when you measure length, weight, or amount.
Use honest scales, honest weights, and honest measures for dry goods and liquids.{n} I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of Egypt.
Keep all my rules and laws, and follow them. I am Yahweh.”

notes.text: Quoted in 1 Peter 1:16.
Hebrew elilim, “nothings” or “worthless things,” a scornful word for idols. It sounds like elohim, “gods.”
Hebrew piggul, meat that has become ritually offensive. See the note at 7:18.
That is, do nothing that puts your neighbor’s life at risk, whether by false testimony or by standing by and doing nothing. The Hebrew is difficult.
Or “so that you do not become guilty because of him” (by letting him go on doing wrong).
Jesus quoted this as the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39; Mark 12:31; Luke 10:27). It is also quoted in Romans 13:9, Galatians 5:14, and James 2:8.
Hebrew shaatnez, a word of uncertain origin that may be foreign. Deuteronomy 22:11 explains it as wool and linen together.
Or “engaged to another man.” The Hebrew word neherepheth is found only here.
Hebrew biqqoret, found only here. It may mean “an inquiry,” “payment,” or “punishment.” The Greek Old Testament reads “they shall be punished.”
Literally “treat its foreskin as its foreskin,” meaning as uncircumcised, or not yet fit for use. The same idea runs through the rest of the verse.
Or “over the blood,” perhaps a ceremony at the place of killing. The Greek Old Testament reads “on the mountains.”
Two kinds of forbidden fortune-telling. The exact practices are uncertain.
Hebrew oboth and yiddeonim, people who ask spirits of the dead for answers and people who claim to have secret knowledge. The exact meanings are uncertain.

Hebrew “an honest ephah and an honest hin.” The ephah was a dry measure of about 3/5 bushel (22 liters), and the hin was a liquid measure of about 1 gallon (3.7 liters). Both stand here for all measures of volume.

subheads.20: A slave woman promised to another man

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: Any Israelite, or foreigner living in Israel, who hands over a child to Molech{a} will be executed. The citizens must stone him to death.
I myself will turn against that man and cut him off from his people, because he gave a child to Molech, which made my holy place unclean and dishonored my holy name.
“Suppose the citizens turn a blind eye when someone gives a child to Molech, and they refuse to execute him.
I will personally oppose that man and his family. Everyone who joins him in unfaithfully worshiping Molech will be cut off from their people, him included.
“If a person goes to mediums and fortune-tellers, giving himself to them like an unfaithful lover, I will turn against him and cut him off from his people.
Make yourselves holy by living set apart, for I am Yahweh your God.
Follow my rules and obey them. I am Yahweh, who makes you holy.
“A person who curses his father or mother is to die. He cursed them, so his blood is on his own head.{b}
“If a man commits adultery with his neighbor’s wife,{c} the penalty is death for the man and for the woman.
A man who sleeps with his father’s wife shames his father. The penalty is death for them both, and the blame is theirs.
A man who sleeps with his daughter-in-law and she with him, are both to die. What they did is twisted, and the blame is theirs.
When one man lies with another as with a woman, each has done something detestable. They must die, and the blame is theirs.
A man who marries a woman and her mother does a shameful wickedness. He and both women are to be burned in a fire, so that none of this wickedness remains among you.
A man who has sex with an animal is to die, and you must kill the animal too.
If a woman approaches an animal to mate with it, kill her and the animal. Both must die, and the blame is theirs.

“A man who marries his sister, the daughter of his father or mother, and they look on each other’s bodies, commits a disgrace.{d} Their people are to cut them off in public view. He has shamed his sister, and he will pay for his wrong.
A man who sleeps with a woman during her monthly bleeding has uncovered her source of blood, and she has allowed it. Their people will cut off both of them.
Never shame your mother’s sister or your father’s sister, for that exposes a close relative. Each of them will pay for the guilt.
A man who sleeps with the wife of his uncle shames his uncle. They will pay for their sin and die with no children.
A man who takes his brother’s wife does an impure thing.{e} He has shamed his brother, and the couple will stay childless.
“Keep all my rules and laws, and obey them. If you do not, the land where I am bringing you to live will throw you out.
Do not live by the customs of the nations I am driving out ahead of you. They did all of these things, which is why I came to hate them.
I have already promised you: you will take over their land. I will give it to you as your own, a land full of milk and honey. I am Yahweh your God, who has set you apart from other peoples.

So tell clean animals from unclean ones, and unclean birds from clean ones. Do not make yourselves hateful by eating any animal, bird, or creature that crawls on the ground, since I have marked these as unclean for you.
You are to be holy to me. I, Yahweh, am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations so that you belong to me.
“Any man or woman who is a medium or fortune-teller{f} is to be executed by stoning, and the blame is theirs.”

notes.text: See the note at 18:21. Here the Greek Old Testament reads Moloch.
That is, he is responsible for his own death. The same idea is used throughout this chapter.
The repeated clause may be an accidental copying mistake. The Greek Old Testament reads “Whoever commits adultery with the wife of a man, or whoever commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor.”
Hebrew hesed, usually “steadfast love,” used here in a rare negative sense, “shame.”
Hebrew niddah, the word used for the impurity of a woman’s monthly period.
Literally “in whom there is a medium (ov) or a spirit of knowing.” See the note at 19:31.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses, “Give this message to the priests, the descendants of Aaron: No priest may become unclean by going near a dead body among his people,
with these exceptions, his nearest family:{a} mother, father, son, daughter, and brother,
along with a sister who is unmarried and still lives with him. For her, he may become unclean.
As a husband, he must not become unclean for his wife’s relatives and so shame himself.{b}
Priests must not shave bald patches in their hair, trim off the sides of their beards, or cut their skin.
They belong to their God as holy people and must not disgrace God’s name. They bring Yahweh’s food gifts, the food{c} of their God, and for that reason they must be holy.
Priests may not marry prostitutes or women who have been made unclean by others,{d} or women divorced by their husbands, since a priest is holy to his God.
Count him holy, because it is he who offers the food of your God. To you he is holy, for I, Yahweh, am holy, and I am the one making you holy.
When the daughter of a priest brings shame on herself by working as a prostitute, she brings shame on her father too. Burn her in a fire.
“The high priest, the one raised above his brothers, with anointing oil poured over his head and set apart to wear the special clothes, must never let his hair go loose or rip his clothes.
He must not go near any dead body. Not even for his own father or mother may he make himself unclean.
He must not leave the holy place or treat his God’s holy place as common, because the anointing oil of his God is on him like a crown. I am Yahweh.
The woman he marries has to be a virgin.
A widow, a divorced woman, or a woman made unclean by prostitution is not allowed. He may marry only a virgin from his own people,
so that his children among his people are not dishonored, for I am Yahweh, who makes him holy.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell Aaron: None of your descendants, in any generation, who has a physical defect may come near to offer his God’s food.
No man with a defect may come near. That includes a man who is blind or lame, has a damaged nose,{e} or has a limb that is too long,
a man with a broken foot or a broken hand,
a man with a hunched back or a very small body,{f} a man with a spot in his eye, with skin sores or scabs, or with damaged testicles.
No descendant of Aaron the priest who has a defect may come forward to present Yahweh’s food gifts. Because he has a defect, he may not come near to offer his God’s food.
He may eat his God’s food, both from the most holy offerings and from the holy ones,
but because of his defect he must not go up to the curtain or come near the altar. He would make my holy places{g} common, and I am Yahweh, who makes them holy.”
So Moses gave all this teaching to Aaron, to his sons, and to the whole people of Israel.

notes.text: Literally “his flesh who is near to him.”

The Hebrew is difficult. Literally it says “a husband (or master) must not make himself unclean among his people.” It may mean that a priest must not become unclean for the relatives of his wife, or that as a leader among his people he must not make himself unclean. The Greek Old Testament reads “He shall not make himself unclean suddenly among his people.”
Literally “bread.” It is used this way throughout this chapter and the next.
Or “a woman who has been violated.” The Hebrew halalah means “made common.”
Hebrew harum, perhaps “with a split nose” or some other deformity of the face. The meaning is uncertain.
Or “very thin.” The meanings of several words in this verse are uncertain.
Or “my sanctuaries.” The Greek Old Testament reads “the holy place of his God.”

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell Aaron and his sons to treat with care{a} the holy gifts that the Israelites set apart for me, so that they do not dishonor my holy name. I am Yahweh.
Tell them: If any of your descendants, from now on, comes close to the holy gifts that Israel dedicates to Yahweh while unclean, I will remove him from my presence. I am Yahweh.

No descendant of Aaron who has an unclean skin disease{b} or a bodily flow may eat the holy gifts until he is clean. The same goes for anyone who touches something made unclean by a dead body, or a man who has released semen,
or touches any crawling creature, or any person, that makes him unclean. Whatever the cause may be,
A person who touches any such thing is unclean until evening and may not eat the holy gifts unless he bathes in water first.
After sunset he is clean, and then he may eat the holy gifts. They are his food.
An animal that died on its own or was torn apart by wild animals is not for him to eat, since that would make him unclean. I am Yahweh.
The priests must follow my instructions, so that they do not take on guilt and die for treating the gifts as common. I am Yahweh, who makes them holy.
“No outsider{c} may eat a holy gift. That includes a priest’s guest and a hired worker.
But if a priest buys someone with his own money, that person may eat it, and so may those born in his household.
If a priest’s daughter marries a man who is not a priest, she may not eat the gifts set aside from the holy offerings.
But when a priest’s daughter is left a widow or is divorced without a child, she may come back to her father’s house as in her early years. She then eats of his food. No outsider is ever to eat it.
A man who eats a holy gift by accident must add one fifth of its value and give the gift to the priest.
The priests must not treat as common the holy gifts that the Israelites give to Yahweh,
and so bring guilt on them that calls for a guilt offering{d} by letting them eat the holy gifts. I am Yahweh, who makes them holy.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,

“Tell Aaron, his sons, and every Israelite: When an Israelite or foreigner in Israel brings an offering, whether to keep a promise or as a gift of his own choice, and presents it to Yahweh as a burnt offering,
it must be a male with nothing wrong with it, from the cattle, sheep, or goats, if you want it accepted.
Do not bring anything with a defect. You would not be accepted.

Whoever brings a peace offering to Yahweh, to keep a promise{e} or as a gift of his own choice, from the herd or the flock, must offer an animal with nothing wrong with it so that it is accepted. It must have no defect.
Do not offer Yahweh an animal that is blind, injured, or crippled, or that has running sores, itching skin, or scabs. None of them may be put on Yahweh’s altar as a food gift.
You may offer an ox or lamb whose limb is too long or too short as a gift of your choice, but it will not be accepted for keeping a promise.
Do not give Yahweh any animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut. Do not do this in your land.
Do not take such animals from a foreigner to offer as your God’s food. They are damaged and have defects, so they will not be accepted for you.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“A newborn calf, lamb, or goat stays with its mother for seven days. From the eighth day on, it is acceptable as a food gift to Yahweh.
Never kill a cow or ewe on the same day as her young.
When you bring a thank offering to Yahweh, offer it so that it will be accepted.
It must be eaten that same day, and none of it may be left until morning. I am Yahweh.
“Keep my commands and follow them. I am Yahweh.
You must never treat my holy name with contempt. Among the Israelites I am to be shown as holy. It is I, Yahweh, who set you apart for myself.
He is the one who rescued you from Egypt so he could be your God. I am Yahweh.”

notes.text: Or “deal carefully with.” The Hebrew nazar is related to nazir, “Nazirite,” a person set apart.
Hebrew tsaraat. See the note at 13:2. The Greek Old Testament reads lepra. The condition is not modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease).
Hebrew zar, “stranger,” here anyone who is not from a priestly family.
Hebrew awon ashmah, “guilt of wrongdoing.” See the note on asham at 5:6.
Or “a special promise.” The Hebrew lephalle means “to set apart” or “to make extraordinary.”

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: These are my appointed feasts,{a} the times of Yahweh that you will announce as holy gatherings.
“Work is allowed on six days. The seventh day, though, is a Sabbath, a time of full rest and a holy gathering. Do no work. Wherever you live, it belongs to Yahweh as a Sabbath.
“These are Yahweh’s appointed feasts, the holy gatherings that you will announce at the times set for them.
Yahweh’s Passover{d} comes at twilight{c} on the fourteenth day of the first month (March-April).{b}
The next day, the fifteenth of that month, Yahweh’s Feast of Bread without Yeast starts. Your bread during those seven days must have no yeast in it.
On the first day you hold a holy gathering, and you do no regular work.{e}
For seven days you bring a gift made by fire to Yahweh. The seventh day is another holy gathering, and you do no regular work.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: Once you have come into the land I give you and have reaped its crop, take the first sheaf{f} of your grain to the priest.
He lifts the sheaf in front of Yahweh so that it is accepted for you. The priest does this on the day after the Sabbath.{g}
When the sheaf is lifted, you also sacrifice a male lamb one year old and in perfect condition. It is a burnt offering to Yahweh.
With it goes a grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, about four quarts,{h} a gift made by fire whose smell pleases Yahweh, and a drink offering of wine, about one quart.{i}
Until the day you bring this offering to your God, you may not eat bread, roasted grain, or fresh heads of grain. This is a rule for all time, for your descendants, wherever you live.
“From the day after the Sabbath, the day you brought the sheaf to be lifted up, you count seven full weeks.{j}
You count fifty days, ending on the day following the seventh Sabbath.{k} At that point, present Yahweh with a new grain offering.
From your homes you bring two loaves to be lifted up, each made from about four quarts{l} of fine flour. They are baked with yeast, and are the first part of the harvest for Yahweh.

Present seven perfect lambs a year old, one young bull, and two rams along with the bread. These are a burnt offering for Yahweh, together with the grain and drink offerings that go with them. It is a gift made by fire, and its smell pleases Yahweh.
Offer one male goat for a sin offering, and for a peace offering two male lambs a year old.
The priest lifts them in front of Yahweh along with the bread of the first harvest and the two lambs. They are holy to Yahweh and belong to the priest.
On that very day, you announce a holy gathering and do no regular work. This is a rule for all time, for your descendants, wherever you live.

“At harvest time in your land, leave the edges of the field uncut, and do not go back for the stalks left behind. Those are for poor people and for foreigners who live with you. I am Yahweh your God.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: The seventh month (September-October){m} begins with a day of complete rest. On its first day there is a holy gathering, and horn blasts{n} call it to mind.
You do no regular work, and you bring a gift made by fire to Yahweh.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“The tenth day of this seventh month (September-October){o} is the Day of Atonement.{p} You hold a holy gathering. You humble yourselves{q} and bring a gift made by fire to Yahweh.
You must not work at all on that day, because it is a day when you are made right before Yahweh your God.
Whoever fails to humble himself on that day will be removed from his people.
As for the person who does any work during that day, I will destroy him and remove him from his people.
No work of any kind is allowed. This law stands for all time, for every generation in all your homes.
This is a Sabbath of full rest, and you are to humble yourselves. Observe it from the evening of the ninth day{r} to the evening that follows.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: Starting on the fifteenth day of this seventh month (September-October),{s} Yahweh’s Feast of Booths{t} lasts seven days.
The first day is a holy gathering, and you do no regular work.
Through seven days you present gifts made by fire to Yahweh. The eighth day is one more holy gathering, with a gift made by fire for Yahweh. This closing assembly{u} allows no regular work.
“These are the feasts of Yahweh, the holy gatherings you announce, at which you bring gifts made by fire to Yahweh. Each day has its own burnt offering, grain offering, sacrifice, and drink offering.
These are in addition to Yahweh’s Sabbaths, your other gifts, all your promised offerings, and all the offerings you give freely to Yahweh.
“So from the fifteenth day of the seventh month (September-October),{v} when the crops of the land are in, keep Yahweh’s feast for seven days. Rest completely on the first and the eighth.
On the first day, take fruit from the finest trees,{w} palm branches, leafy branches, and willows from the stream, and for seven days enjoy yourselves in front of Yahweh your God.
Keep this feast for Yahweh one week every year. It is a rule for all time, for your descendants. Celebrate in the seventh month.
Live in booths for those seven days. Every Israelite by birth must live in booths,
so your descendants will remember that when I led the Israelites out of Egypt, I had them live in booths. I am Yahweh your God.”
So Moses announced Yahweh’s appointed feasts to the Israelites.

notes.text: Hebrew moadim, “appointed times,” the set festivals of the year.

Hebrew “in the first month.” The months are counted from the spring start of Israel’s religious year (Exodus 12:2). This month was called Abib (“ripe grain,” Exodus 13:4) and later Nisan (Esther 3:7). The Hebrew months followed the moon, and an extra month was added in some years, so the first month did not match a modern month exactly. It fell in March-April.
Hebrew ben haarbayim, literally “between the two evenings,” the time between sunset and full dark (or, in later practice, between midafternoon and sunset). See the note at Exodus 12:6.
Hebrew pesah, from pasah, “to pass over” (Exodus 12:13, 23, 27).
Literally “work of labor,” meaning a person’s usual job, as different from preparing food (compare Exodus 12:16).
Hebrew omer, a sheaf of grain, here the first sheaf of the barley harvest. Elsewhere the same word is a dry measure (Exodus 16:36).

Which Sabbath is meant was argued in ancient Judaism. The Pharisees and later rabbis took it as the first day of the Feast of Bread without Yeast (the Greek Old Testament reads “the day after the first day”). The Sadducees and others took it as the weekly Sabbath during the feast, so that the count always began on a Sunday.
Hebrew “two tenths,” meaning two tenths of an ephah, about 4.4 liters (4 quarts).
Hebrew “a fourth of a hin,” about 0.9 liter (1 quart).
Or “seven full weeks.”
This day, the Feast of Weeks (Exodus 34:22; Deuteronomy 16:10), is called Pentecost in Greek, meaning “fiftieth” (Acts 2:1).
Hebrew “two tenths,” meaning two tenths of an ephah, about 4.4 liters (4 quarts).

Hebrew “in the seventh month,” counted from the spring start of the year and later called Tishri (1 Kings 8:2 calls it Ethanim). The Hebrew months followed the moon, so it fell in September-October. In later Judaism this first day became Rosh Hashanah, the civil New Year.
Hebrew teruah, a shout or blast, usually understood as the sound of the shofar (ram’s horn). The Greek Old Testament reads “a memorial of trumpets.”
Hebrew “the tenth day of this seventh month” (Tishri). See the note at verse 24.
Hebrew yom hakkippurim, “day of atonements,” or Yom Kippur. See chapter 16.
Literally “afflict your souls.” See the note at 16:29. The same words are used in verses 29 and 32.
Since the Hebrew day began at sunset, the observance runs from the evening that ends the ninth day to the evening of the tenth.
Hebrew “the fifteenth day of this seventh month” (Tishri). See the note at verse 24.
Hebrew sukkot, “booths” or “huts,” temporary shelters made of branches. Traditionally called the Feast of Tabernacles.
Hebrew atseret, perhaps “closing assembly.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a time of release.”
Hebrew “the fifteenth day of the seventh month” (Tishri). See the note at verse 24.
Hebrew ets hadar, “splendid trees,” identified in Jewish tradition as the citron (etrog).

subheads.4: Passover and the Feast of Bread without Yeast

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Command the Israelites to supply you with clear oil pressed from olives, to keep the lamp lit{a} always.

Aaron is to set up the lamps outside the curtain in front of the covenant chest in the meeting tent, so that they burn in front of Yahweh from evening until morning, always. This is a rule for all time, for your descendants.
He is to keep the lamps on the pure gold lampstand{b} in front of Yahweh at all times.
“Take fine flour and bake twelve loaves{c} from it, each made from about four quarts.{d}
Set them on the pure gold table in front of Yahweh in two rows, six in each row.{e}
Put pure frankincense beside each row, to be the reminder portion{f} for the bread, a gift made by fire to Yahweh.
Every Sabbath, Aaron sets out fresh bread in front of Yahweh. It is a lasting agreement from the Israelites.
The bread belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place. It is most holy for them, taken from the gifts made by fire to Yahweh, and it is theirs for all time.”
One man had an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father. He went out into the camp among the Israelites, and a fight broke out between him and another Israelite.
The Israelite woman’s son cursed and spoke evil of the Name.{g} He was taken to Moses. (His mother’s name was Shelomith,{h} and she was Dibri’s daughter,{i} of the tribe of Dan.){j}
He was kept under guard while they waited to learn Yahweh’s will.
Then Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Bring the cursing man out beyond the camp. All who heard him are to place their hands on his head, and then everyone in the community will stone him.
Tell the Israelites: If someone curses his God, he carries the guilt for his sin.
Anyone who speaks against Yahweh’s name must be put to death, and the whole community is to stone him. Whether he is a foreigner or native-born, if he speaks against the Name, he must die.
“If anyone takes a human life, he is to be executed.
If anyone takes an animal’s life, he pays for it with another animal.
If a man hurts another person, what he did will be done to him:
a break for a break, an eye lost for an eye, a tooth lost for a tooth.{k} He is to suffer the same harm he did to the other person.
Killing an animal calls for repayment. Killing a person calls for death.
The law is the same for the foreigner as for the native. I am Yahweh your God.”
Moses repeated this to the Israelites. They brought the cursing man out of the camp and killed him with stones. The Israelites carried out Yahweh’s command to Moses exactly.

notes.text: Literally “to cause a lamp to go up.”
Literally “the pure lampstand,” meaning the lampstand of pure gold (Exodus 25:31).
Or “twelve rings of bread,” the bread of the Presence (Exodus 25:30).
Hebrew “two tenths,” meaning two tenths of an ephah, about 4.4 liters (4 quarts).
Or “in two piles, six to a pile.”
Hebrew azkarah. See the note at 2:2.

Hebrew hashshem, “the Name,” meaning the name Yahweh (verse 16). From this passage comes the Jewish custom of saying HaShem, “the Name,” in place of the divine name. The Greek Old Testament reads “named the Name.”
Shelomith means “peaceful,” from shalom, “peace.” The Greek Old Testament spells it Salomith.
Dibri may mean “talkative” or “my word.” The Greek Old Testament spells it Dabri.
Dan means “judge” (Genesis 30:6).

This rule of equal payment (the Latin name is lex talionis) set a limit on punishment. It was applied by judges and was not for private revenge. Compare Exodus 21:23-25; Deuteronomy 19:21; Matthew 5:38-39.

subheads.10: A man who cursed God’s name
subheads.13: Punishment for the one who cursed

verses.text: On Mount Sinai Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites: After you come into the land I am giving you, the land itself must have a Sabbath rest for Yahweh.
For six years, plant your fields, trim your vineyards, and bring in what they produce.
The seventh year is different. It is a Sabbath year of full rest for the land, a rest for Yahweh. Do not plant your fields or trim your vineyards.
Do not harvest whatever grows on its own from the last crop, and do not pick grapes from the vines you left untrimmed.{a} The land is to have a year of full rest.
Whatever the land grows during the Sabbath year can be food for all of you: you, your male and female slaves, your hired workers, and the foreigners living with you,
and also your livestock and the wild animals of your land. Everything it grows may be eaten.
“Count seven Sabbath years, seven sevens, a total of forty-nine years.
When that time is up, on the tenth day of the seventh month (September-October),{b} sound the loud horn.{c} On the Day of Atonement, let the horn be heard across your whole country.
Make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim freedom{d} throughout the land to all its people. It will be a jubilee{e} for you, when every person returns to the family land and to the clan.
That fiftieth year is your jubilee. Do not plant, do not gather what grows by itself, and do not pick grapes from the vines nobody trimmed.
Because it is a jubilee, it is holy to you. You may eat whatever the fields produce.
In this jubilee year, everyone is to go back to his own property.
When you sell something to a neighbor or buy something from one, do not cheat each other.
What you pay your neighbor depends on how many years have passed since the jubilee, and what he charges you depends on how many crop years remain.
When many years remain, raise the price. When few years remain, lower it. What he actually sells you is a count of harvests.
Do not take advantage of one another. Fear your God, for I am Yahweh your God.
“Obey my laws and keep my rulings, and you will be secure in the land.
The land will give its crops, you will eat all you want, and nothing will threaten you there.
You may ask, ‘What will we eat in the seventh year, if we cannot plant or gather crops?’
In the sixth year I will send a blessing so rich that the crop will last three years.
You will plant in the eighth year and still be eating from the old crop. Until the new harvest comes in during the ninth year, you will live on the old grain.
“Land may never be sold for good,{f} because the land is mine. In my eyes you are only foreigners and guests.
In all the land you own, you must allow the land to be bought back.
“If one of your relatives becomes poor and has to sell part of his land, his closest family redeemer{g} comes and buys back what his relative sold.
If a man has no one to buy it back, but he later does well and gets enough money to do so,
he counts the years since the sale, pays the buyer for the years left, and returns to his land.
But if he cannot get enough to pay him back, what he sold stays with the buyer until the jubilee year. Then it is released, and he goes back to his land.
“If a man sells a house inside a walled town, he can buy it back at any point during the first full year{h} after he sells it.
If it is not bought back before that year ends, the house in the walled town belongs to the buyer for good, and to his descendants. It is not released at the jubilee.
Houses in villages with no wall are treated as part of the open country. They can be bought back, and the jubilee releases them.
Levites hold a permanent right to buy back their houses in the towns they own.
If a Levite does not buy back{i} a house, it is still released in the jubilee, because the houses in the Levites’ towns are their property among the Israelites.
The open pastureland around their towns must never be sold. It is theirs for all time.
“If a relative of yours becomes poor and cannot make a living{j} among you, help him. Let him live with you like a foreigner or guest.
Do not charge him interest or make a profit from him.{k} Honor your God, and let your relative live alongside you.
Do not lend him money with interest, and do not sell him food to make a profit.
I am Yahweh your God. Getting you out of Egypt was meant to put Canaan in your hands, with me as your God.
“If a poor relative of yours sells himself to you, you may not make him serve as a slave.
Treat him as a hired worker or a guest, serving you only until the jubilee year.
Then he and his children are free to leave you and go back to his own family and the land his ancestors held.
They are my servants, whom I rescued from Egypt, so they may not be sold the way slaves are sold.
Do not govern him with cruelty. Honor your God.
Your male and female slaves must come from the nations around you. Those are the people you may buy as slaves.
You may also buy children of the foreigners residing among you, along with their families who were born in your land. Such people can become your property,
and you may pass them on to your children, who will own them permanently. But never treat your fellow Israelites harshly.
“Suppose a foreigner living among you gets rich, and a poor relative of yours sells himself to that foreigner or to someone in his family.
Once he has sold himself, the right to buy him back stays with him. A brother of his may pay the price,
or his uncle, or his cousin, or any close relative in his clan. If he becomes well off, he can buy himself back.
He and his buyer count the years from when he sold himself until the jubilee year. The price is set by the number of years, as if he were a hired worker for that time.
If many years remain, he pays back part of his purchase price in proportion to those years.
If only a few years remain before the jubilee, he works out the amount with his owner and pays his price back in proportion to the years left.
He lives with his owner like a worker hired from year to year. His owner must not rule over him harshly while you watch.
If he is not bought back in any of these ways, he and his children go free in the jubilee year.
The Israelites are servants of mine. They are the ones I freed from Egypt, and they are mine. I am Yahweh your God.”

notes.text: Hebrew nazir, literally “your Nazirite,” meaning a vine left untrimmed, like the uncut hair of a Nazirite (Numbers 6:5).

Hebrew “in the seventh month, on the tenth of the month,” counted from the spring start of the religious year. The month was later called Tishri. Because the months followed the moon, it fell in September-October. See the notes at 16:29 and 23:24.
Hebrew shofar teruah, “a horn of blasting,” the ram’s horn.
Hebrew deror, a legal word for release from debt and slavery. These words are carved on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia. Compare Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18-19.

Hebrew yovel, “ram” or “ram’s horn,” named for the horn blown to announce the year. The Latin word jubilaeus, from which “jubilee” comes, was influenced by jubilare, “to shout for joy.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a year of release.”
Hebrew litsmitut, “for complete cutting off,” meaning beyond the right to be bought back.
Hebrew goel, the nearest relative, responsible to buy back property and persons and to take revenge for a killing (Ruth 3:12-13; Numbers 35:19).
Literally “days.”
The Hebrew is hard to understand. The Latin Vulgate reads “If it is not bought back,” which fits the context, and many interpreters add a negative.
Literally “his hand falters.”
Hebrew neshek and tarbit, probably interest taken in advance (literally “bite”) and interest added at repayment.

verses.text: “Do not make idols{a} for yourselves. Do not set up a carved figure or a sacred pillar, and do not put a carved stone{b} anywhere in your land to bow down to. I am Yahweh your God.
Keep my Sabbaths and show respect for my holy place. I am Yahweh.{c}
“If you live by my laws, obey my commands, and put them into practice,
Your rains will arrive in their proper seasons. The fields will yield grain, and fruit will hang on the orchard trees.
Threshing will last into the grape season, and the grape season into sowing time. Bread will be plentiful and your land will be a safe place to live.
I will give your land peace, and you will lie down to sleep with nothing to fear. I will rid the land of dangerous animals, and no army will march through your country.
You will pursue your enemies, and they will drop under your blades.
Five of you will put a hundred to flight, and when a hundred of you face ten thousand, they too will run. Your enemies will be cut down in front of you.
I will look on you with favor, make you have many children, and keep my agreement with you.
Last year’s grain will still be in your storehouses when you must clear it out for the new crop.
I will make my home{d} among you and will never push you away.
I will be present with you wherever you go. You will be my people, and I will be your God.{e}
I am Yahweh your God, the one who took you out of Egypt and ended your slavery there. I snapped the bars of your yoke and let you stand tall.
“But if you will not listen to me and refuse to carry out all these commands,
if you turn down my laws and despise my rulings, so that you break my agreement and fail to keep all my commands,

I will deal with you like this: sudden terror will come on you, with wasting sickness and burning fever that dim the eyes and sap your strength. Your seed will be planted for nothing, since your enemies will eat what grows.
I will turn my face against you. You will lose battles to your enemies, and those who hate you will govern you. You will flee at the sound of nothing, with no pursuer in sight.
“If you still refuse to obey me after all that, I will make your punishment seven times heavier.
I will break your proud strength. Above you the sky will be hard as iron, and beneath you the earth as hard as bronze.
Your effort will be wasted. The soil will give no crops, and the orchard trees will bear no fruit.
“If you stand against{f} me and refuse to listen, I will multiply the blows on you by seven, matching your sins.
I will send wild animals among you to carry off your children, kill your cattle, and leave you so few that your roads are empty.
“If even these things do not correct you and you keep opposing me,
I will then be against you as well, and I will hit you seven times harder for your sins.
Next I will send an army against you to carry out the penalty of my agreement. When you pull back into your cities, I will send disease among you and let your enemies take you.
When I cut off your supply of bread,{g} ten women will bake for you in a single oven. They will hand it out in measured portions, and you will eat without being satisfied.
“If you still will not listen after that, and go on opposing me,
I will turn against you in burning anger and give you a punishment seven times as severe for your sins.
You will end up eating your own sons and daughters.
I will wreck your hilltop shrines, chop down your incense stands,{h} and stack your corpses on the broken remains of your idols.{i} I will find you disgusting.
I will turn your cities into rubble and wreck your holy places. I will take no pleasure in the smell of your offerings.
I will make your land a wasteland, and the enemies who come to live in it will stare in horror.
I will scatter you among the nations and chase you with a drawn sword. Your land will be empty and your cities ruined.
“Then the land will make up{j} for its Sabbaths during all the time it lies empty and you are living in your enemies’ land. The land will rest and pay back its Sabbaths.
For all the days it lies empty, it will have the rest your Sabbaths never gave it while you were living on it.{k}
Those who are left will have their courage drained away in enemy territory. A rustling leaf will set them running. They will run as if from a sword, and stumble even though nobody follows.
You will trip over each other as if running from a sword, though nobody is chasing you. You will be unable to stand against your enemies.
You will vanish among the nations, and your enemies’ country will consume you.
Those left alive will waste away in enemy lands because of their own guilt, and with them because of their ancestors’ guilt.
“But if they admit their guilt and the guilt of their ancestors, the way they betrayed me and opposed me,
so that I opposed them and took them into the land of their enemies, and if their stubborn hearts are then humbled and they accept the penalty for their guilt,{l}
then I will recall what I promised Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham,{m} and I will think of the land.
For the land will be left behind by them, and while it lies empty without them it will make up for its Sabbaths. They will pay for their guilt, because they threw out my rulings and hated my laws.
Even so, while they are in enemy country, I will neither throw them out nor despise them to the point of wiping them out, which would break my agreement with them. I am Yahweh their God.
Because of them, I will recall the agreement made with their ancestors, the people I led from Egypt as the nations watched, to be their God. I am Yahweh.”
These are the regulations, rulings, and laws Yahweh established with the Israelites at Mount Sinai, with Moses as go-between.

notes.text: Hebrew elilim, “worthless things.” See the note at 19:4.
Hebrew even maskit, perhaps a stone carved with figures. The meaning is uncertain.

Part of the Greek text of this chapter (verses 2-16) survives in a scroll from Qumran, 4QLXXLev-a, one of the oldest known manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament. Its wording differs from the standard Greek text at several points.
Hebrew mishkan, “tabernacle.” The Greek Old Testament reads “my tabernacle,” and some ancient copies read “my covenant.”
Quoted in 2 Corinthians 6:16.
Hebrew qeri, found only in this chapter (verses 21-41), perhaps “in hostility” or “at random” (by chance, as if I did not matter).
Literally “break your staff of bread.”
Hebrew hammanim, perhaps incense altars or sun pillars. The Greek Old Testament reads “wooden images made with hands.”
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous word for idols, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Or “pay off” or “enjoy.” The Hebrew ratsah is the verb used for the acceptance of sacrifices. It appears again in verses 41 and 43.
Compare 2 Chronicles 36:21.
Or “they accept their punishment for their guilt.” The same applies in verse 43.

The patriarchs are listed in reverse order: Jacob, Isaac, Abraham. Their names are explained in Genesis: Abraham, “father of a multitude” (17:5); Isaac, “he laughs” (21:6); Jacob, “he grasps the heel” (25:26).

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites: When someone makes a special promise{a} to Yahweh to give a person, the price you set for that person is as follows.
For a male between twenty and sixty years old, the price is about 20 ounces of silver,{b} weighed by the standard of the holy place.{c}
For a female, the price is about 12 ounces.{d}
For a person between five and twenty years old, the price is about 8 ounces for a male and about 4 ounces for a female.{e}
For a person from one month to five years old, the price is about 2 ounces of silver for a male and about 1.2 ounces of silver for a female.{f}
For a person sixty or older, the price is about 6 ounces for a male and about 4 ounces for a female.{g}
If the one who made the promise is too poor to pay the price, he is brought to the priest, who sets a sum according to his means.
“If the promise is an animal of the kind that can be brought to Yahweh as an offering, whatever he gives to Yahweh becomes holy.
He may not swap it or trade it for another, whether better or worse. If he does trade one animal for another, both animals become holy.
If the animal is unclean, the kind that cannot be offered to Yahweh, he brings it to the priest,
who decides whether it is good or poor. The priest’s decision stands.
If the owner wants to buy it back, he adds one fifth to the price.
“When a man makes his house holy for Yahweh, the priest decides if it is good or poor. The price the priest sets is the price.
If the man who set apart the house wants it back, he adds one fifth to the price and the house is his again.
“If a man sets apart to Yahweh some of the land he owns, the price depends on the seed it takes to plant it. A field needing about 6 bushels{h} of barley seed is priced at about 20 ounces of silver.
If he sets apart his field right after a jubilee year, the full price stands.
If he sets it apart after the jubilee, the priest figures the price according to the years left until the next jubilee, and the price is lowered.
If the man who set the field apart wants to buy it back, he adds one fifth to the price, and it is his again.
But if he does not buy it back, or if he sells it to someone else, it is gone for good.
When the field is released at the jubilee, it becomes holy to Yahweh, like a field given over for good.{i} It belongs to the priest.
If a man sets apart to Yahweh a field he bought, one that is not part of his family land,
the priest figures the price up to the next jubilee, and the man pays that price on the same day as a holy gift to Yahweh.
In the jubilee year the field goes back to the person he bought it from, the one whose land it was.
Every price is set by the standard of the holy place.{j}
“No one may set apart a firstborn animal, because the firstborn already belongs to Yahweh. Whether it is a cow or a sheep, it is Yahweh’s.
If it is an unclean animal, the owner may buy it back at the price you set, plus one fifth. If it is not bought back, it is sold at your price.”
“Nothing that a person gives over to Yahweh from what he owns, whether a person, an animal, or a family field, may be sold or bought back. Everything given over is most holy to Yahweh.
No human being given over to destruction{k} can be bought back. He must die.
“A tenth of everything the land produces, from seed in the ground or from the fruit trees, belongs to Yahweh. It is holy to Yahweh.
If a man wants to buy back some of his tenth, he adds one fifth to its value.
Every tenth animal of the herd or flock, counted as it passes under the shepherd’s staff,{l} is holy to Yahweh.
He may not check whether it is good or bad, and he may not trade it. If he does trade it, both animals become holy, and neither can be bought back.”
Such were the commandments Yahweh handed to Moses at Mount Sinai for the Israelites.

notes.text: Or “an extraordinary promise.” See the note at 22:21. People promised to Yahweh (compare 1 Samuel 1:11) were bought back by paying their price to the holy place.

Hebrew “fifty shekels of silver.” The shekel was a unit of weight, about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams). Fifty shekels were about 20 ounces (575 grams). The Greek Old Testament reads “didrachms” throughout this chapter.
Literally “by the shekel of the holy place,” the official standard weight. See verse 25.
Hebrew “thirty shekels,” about 12 ounces (345 grams).
Hebrew “twenty shekels” (about 8 ounces, 230 grams) and “ten shekels” (about 4 ounces, 115 grams).
Hebrew “five shekels” (about 2 ounces, 57.5 grams) and “three shekels” (about 1.2 ounces, 34.5 grams).
Hebrew “fifteen shekels” (about 6 ounces, 172.5 grams) and “ten shekels” (about 4 ounces, 115 grams).
Hebrew “a homer,” a dry measure of about 6 bushels (about 220 liters), probably first a donkey load (Hebrew hamor, “donkey”). The price is “fifty shekels of silver,” about 20 ounces (575 grams).
Hebrew herem, something given over to Yahweh for good, either to the holy place or to destruction. See verses 28-29.
Hebrew “the shekel of the holy place; twenty gerahs are to be the shekel.” The gerah was the smallest weight, one twentieth of a shekel, about 0.02 ounce (0.6 gram).
Or “who has been given over” (Hebrew herem). This means people condemned under the ban, as in Deuteronomy 13:12-18 and Joshua 6:17, not people promised in verses 2-8.
Literally “passes under the rod,” the way a shepherd counts his flock (Jeremiah 33:13; Ezekiel 20:37).
